speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I find that one of the committees of the house, the standing committee on veterans affairs, in submitting its report to the house on July 1 ascribed to me a statement which is not in accord with the information which I communicated to the committee in question. The report of the committee, which is to be found on page 639 of Votes and Proceedings of that day, in paragraph 14 refers to information which is ascribed to me on the present state of the war claims fund, and states that I had told the committee that the sum of $6 million remains in the fund.
That is not a correct statement at all, Mr. Speaker, of the information I communicated to the committee. The information was contained in a letter dated April 10, 1959, which I wrote to the chairman of the committee and which I believe became part of the records of the committee. There I indicated that the combined cash and market value of the bonds held to the credit of the fund at that date was about $4.6 million. I may say further, Mr. Speaker, that since that time there have been, of course, substantial disbursements out of the fund and the balance today is approximately $4 million.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INQUIRY INTO TREATIES RESPECTING RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the governor in council has appointed a commission under the Inquiries Act to inquire into the implementation of treaties 8 and 11 respecting the 15 Indian bands of the Mackenzie district, and to report its recommendations after full consultation with the Indians concerned. Under the terms of the treaties these 15 Indian bands, numbering approximately 4,500 people, have a total land settlement of some 576,000 acres. The rapid development of the Northwest Territories makes it imperative that the land provided for the establishment of reserves be set aside for that purpose now or, alternatively, that the treaties be renegotiated with the consent of the Indians. The commission will consider the present and future economic and social welfare of the Indians and will obtain the views of each band on all aspects of the matter.
The commission consists of five members: Chairman, Mr. Walter H. Nelson, barrister, Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Mr. V. F. Valentine, Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, Ottawa; Mr. L. L. Brown, Indian affairs branch, Department of Citizenship and Immigration, Ottawa; Mr. James Koe, Fort McPherson band, Fort McPherson, Northwest Territories and Mr. Baptiste Ca-zon, Fort Simpson band, Fort Simpson, Northwest Territories.
The commission began its meetings in Aklavik on July 6, 1959.

In answer to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and also because of the concern that has been expressed by all members from the province of British Columbia, I should like to inform the house what has happened in this situation.
On July 7 the Canada labour relations board rejected an application made by an officer of the S.I.U. on behalf of a number of marine engineers for the decertification of the national association of marine engineers as bargaining agent for the engineering officers employed by the company. At the same time the board granted a request of the S.I.U. that its own application for certification as bargaining agent be withdrawn.
Pending release of the board's decision on the proceedings before it, the N.A.M.E. had been enjoined by court order from picketing the company's operations. When the N.A.M.E. resumed its picketing the S.I.U. withdrew men who had been supplied to replace the longshoremen members of the international longshoremen and warehousemen's union who usually performed such work. As a result the company was unable to load its facilities.
The deck officers and masters employed by the company who are members of the Canadian merchant service guild, are reported to have left their employment on July 7. While there is still a confused situation affecting this coastal shipping operation, with court actions and proceedings involving the B.C. federation of labour, the I.L.W.U. and other labour organizations and individuals, the situation should become clearer since the application for decertification has been disposed of and the employer should now feel free to negotiate a settlement with the certified bargaining agent. Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, arising out of the widespread discrimination in quotas in Manitoba and Saskatchewan where, on July 6, 90 per cent and 80 per cent respectively were below 7 bushels. Can the minister say what extraordinary action will be taken to equalize those quotas with the end of the crop year just three weeks away?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
My hon. friend with his use of "widespread discrimination" is attempting to convey the impression that something is being done which should not be done, and he is creating his usual state of alarm. The situation with regard to quotas out west is vastly improved over what it was last year, and I regret that the hon. member does not draw attention to that fact on some of the occasions that arise here in the house. Last year, on July 6, all the stations were on 5 and 6 bushel quotas. On July 6 of this year 775 stations were already on the 7 and 8 bushel quotas and 1,246 were on 5 and 6 bushel quotas, and there are only seven stations remaining on the 4 bushel quota. No attempt is being made at discrimination; an attempt is being made at enlarging the delivery of grain out west and there is still a chance, as expressed by the wheat board, of bringing all the stations out west up to a 7 and 8 bushel quota this year.
The situation does not differ materially from what it was in July a year ago when the quota was raised to 7 for half the stations. Then, I think, my hon. friend complained because some were still on 6, but generally the picture is quite good. There has been a slowing down in some areas out west for reasons which are well known to the house. The lake shipping season is not as good for grain this year as it was last year; consequently some millions of bushels have not been moved from the lakehead, opening terminal capacity for shipments from the southern parts of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. But the month of July is usually a month of large shipments from the lakehead, and we still have some time before the end of the crop year. I repeat that everything is being done not to create discrimination at the many delivery points but to bring them all up to the same level.

Mr. Speaker, how does the minister claim that there is less discrimination this year, or that the situation is better


this year, when last year there was a spread between delivery quotas of only 1 bushel, whereas the spread this year is very wide? Does the minister say now that within a three week period all quotas on the prairies will be 7 or 8 bushels? If this is his answer, I am perfectly satisfied.

That was the estimate given by the members of the wheat board when they were here before the agriculture committee of the house two weeks ago. I am quite free to admit that there is a gap between those now on 5, 6 and 8. Last year none was on the 8 bushel quota, but the board think they will all be on 7 or 8 this year, which is an improvement over last year.
Can the minister say whether he expects any acceleration of shipments through the lakehead now 60 million bushels under last year.

Quite a large proportion of lake shipping has been utilized this season for the shipment of iron ore, in view of the anticipated steel strike, and not so many ships were made available for the movement of wheat; but within the last few days there has been an increase in the movement of wheat from the lakehead. Care is being taken-I spoke to the Minister of Transport about this-to see that those grain ships are not delayed in their passage through the Welland canal.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: LIST OF ORDERS OF THE HOUSE STILL OUTSTANDING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is customary at this time for the minister responsible for this department to review the progress made and to deal with the various aspects of the work of the department, and I propose to do so briefly. I am particularly pleased to have the opportunity to do so this year because since the end of last session I have been able to visit most of the district offices of the department, as well as our treatment institutions across the country.
I may say, Mr. Chairman, that I have found this a most interesting and enlightening experience, and it has given me a much more accurate perspective of the work carried out by the department in looking after veterans problems in the field. In the light of my own experience I am convinced that very few hon. members are fully aware of what is actually involved in the administration of the so-called veterans charter. I believe, therefore, that it would be useful to the committee to get a first-hand report of what I have been privileged to see.
While it is true that the estimates of the department have already been before the standing committee on veterans affairs and that some of this information was given to that committee, I think other members will be interested in it as well. Incidentally, I should like to express my appreciation to the chairman and the members of the standing committee for the excellent work which they are again doing in the interest of our veterans. Previous committees have set a high standard of good will and co-operation in this respect, and the present committee has more than upheld this tradition.
I should like to deal first with the administration of the Pension Act. In my travels across the country and in my personal contacts I have been greatly heartened by the
Supply-Veterans Affairs expressions of confidence which I have received both as to the provisions of the legislation itself and its administration. I have said that in these matters there is no finality, no closed door. It is my hope that in the not too distant future, next session in fact, we shall again bring this legislation before the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs with a view to being assured that our legislation shall not fall short of our intent.
All of us who have been close to this national undertaking are aware that its object is to seek to assure that no Canadian who has suffered a disability in mind or body arising out of his military service or, in the case of combat service, incurred during such service, shall be denied such measure of assistance as may be possible under the act. Parliament in its wisdom having enacted legislation, has deliberately removed its administration from the sphere of personal or political influence. The pension commission has been given the dual responsibility of interpreting and administering the act. By statute there is no appeal from its decision; that is to say, in so far as the Pension Act is concerned an appeal board of the commission is the court of last resort.
The administration of the Pension Act is big business even in this era of large expenditures. The committee will be interested to know that the current budget of the Canadian pension commission is $151,474,000. There are currently 187,015 pensions in payment, including awards to dependants. You will not be surprised to learn that there is a constantly growing rate of decline in the number of pensions payable for service in world war I. The years are taking their toll of both pensioners and their wives. The number of children currently of age for additional pension is declining sharply at the same time.
For this reason mainly the current liability for world war I is shrinking each year and at an accelerated rate. At the same time the world war II liability continues to increase and presumably will continue to do so for some years to come. However, despite the most recent increases in the rate of pension awards and the current increases on world war II account, there has been a slight overall reduction in the total liability in the last two years. This must not be attributed to any lessening of benefits or narrowing of the qualifications for entitlement. On the contrary, the actual benefits to the individual pensioner have been materially increased during this period.
I should like to say a few words, Mr. Chairman, with reference to war veterans allowances. The general administration of the War

Supply-Veterans Affairs Veterans Allowance Act is under the jurisdiction of the minister except as to the authority to deal with and adjudicate upon applications made under the act. This authority is vested in a board located in Ottawa and in the district authorities which are established in each district of the department across Canada. The district authorities and the veterans welfare services in the districts constitute a field force which handles the processing of applications and reviews, arranges for medical examinations when indicated and performs all other duties pertinent to the adjudication of applications for war veterans allowances.
It might be of interest to mention that from the inception of the legislation in 1930 until 1950 inclusive, a period of 20 years, the total number of recipients had reached 33,877. Since 1950 the recipient strength has increased to 64,904, or almost doubled. The expenditures for the year 1950-51, inclusive of the assistance fund, amounted to $23,655,155, and in the fiscal year 1958-59, seven years later, these expenditures totalled $56,966,263. It will be seen that the work load of war veterans allowances in the districts has considerably increased. The number of approved applications at present averages 800 per month.
I might point out that this act was amended at the first session of the 23rd parliament in 1957. The basic rate of allowances payable to a single recipient was increased from $720 to $840 a year and the permissible ceiling of income for a single recipient was increased from $960 to $1,080 a year. The ceiling for a recipient at the married rate was increased from $1,620 to $1,740, and for a recipient with a blind spouse from $1,740 to $1,860 a year. All these increases were effective from November 1, 1957.
There are approximately 3,000 recipients who have become eligible for allowance because of these increases. In addition, the eligibility for war veterans allowance was at the same time extended to Canadian veterans who saw at last 365 days of service in the United Kingdom during world war I, and eligibility was also granted to the widows of deceased veterans who would have qualified on this basis. Some 967 additional recipients have been granted allowances because of this extension of eligibility. Also, the period of residence in Canada required of imperial and allied veterans of world war I and earlier conflicts, and their widows, in order to qualify for the allowance was reduced from 20 to 10 years, and a great many recipients have qualified as a result of this reduced residence requirement. The additional annual allowance payable because of these various amendments to the act is estimated at $10 million.


Two further amendments improved the position of a number of recipients because of the increased length of permissible absence from Canada from three to six months in a year, and an increase in the permissible equity in a home occupied by a recipient from $6,000 to $8,000.
I should like to say a few words now with reference to the Veterans' Land Act. As hon. members know, the Veterans' Land Act was amended this year, and the amendments were very thoroughly discussed at the time the resolution and bill were before the house and also in the veterans affairs committee. I will make a brief summary of the activities and achievements of the Veterans' Land Act administration.
Up until the end of March, 1959, 77,187 veterans had been settled under the act, 33,395 as full-time farmers, 42,680 as small holder and 1,112 as commercial fishermen. This had involved a total public expenditure of $389,738,861 for land, livestock and equipment. Of this amount $191,760,874 was still outstanding and annual collections amount to $21,244,736. Including prepayments on account, 105.8 per cent of all principal and interest due and owing had been collected by March 31, 1959.
Of the 77,187 settled, 16,297 had already repaid their indebtedness and received title to their properties; 5,210 had transferred their equity in their properties to other veterans who became established under the act; 2,038 had quitclaimed their properties back to the director, some due to failure to find a satisfactory way of life in farming and some for strictly administrative or other reasons; 638 had vacated provincial land on which they had been settled by their provinces and toward whose settlement the Veterans' Land Act had made a contribution. Of the 77,187 settled only 186, or less than three out of every thousand, had to be put off their property for failure to live up to their contracts.
Under the home construction program a total of 26,423 homes had been built, or were under construction, at March, 1959. A large majority of these homes have been built by the veterans themselves acting as their own contractors under supervision by Veterans' Land Act construction supervisors, and after attending a Veterans' Land Act construction school. A total of over 700 construction schools have been held since the first one organized in 1949. Under this plan veterans have built, or are building, their own homes at a very considerable saving to themselves, and now have homes of their own which in many cases would otherwise have been impossible.

The measure of success achieved by this branch of the department should not be considered only in terms of collections, but in the rehabilitation service extended in helping former comrades meet and solve their problems and in the contribution being made to the agricultural industry as a whole. The advice given to settlers has not been restricted to line fences but, from reports I have from all over the country as well as from my own observations, 1 know that valuable information is being passed along to many others engaged in agriculture.
Canada is justifiably proud of its record in successfully rehabilitating in civil life several hundred thousands of its sons and daughters who served the nation so well during world war II. The great majority of these have put to excellent use the opportunities and resources provided by our legislation. They are now making a solid contribution to the Canadian way of life and are not asking for further help. However, there is a significant number of veterans and their dependents not only from world war II but also from world war I and earlier military efforts, for whom we carry a continuing and, in some areas, an increasing responsibility. It is with these that our welfare services branch is especially concerned.
The continuing work of rehabilitating the casualties of war is a primary responsibility. Battle disabilities and service diseases may be medically repaired or cured but the physical impairment remains, and may at any time give way under the excessive stress and pressures of modern life. The department knows from experience that the vast majority of disabled veterans can be efficient and reliable workers when trained and placed in jobs within their intellectual and physical abilities. But experience also discloses that disabilities may be aggravated by many post-war causes, and the appropriate job of today is not necessarily suitable tomorrow.
The need for maintaining casualty rehabilitation service is borne out by the steady volume of new and reopened cases. Over the past five years the average number of active casualty cases under service at all times has been approximately 4,600. Departmental activity reports clearly indicate that in the foreseeable future there will be little or no reduction in this figure, and it therefore follows that services for Canada's war disabled will be required on a continuous basis.
In the district office the administrative and field work related to war veterans allowance and the supplementary benefits provided by the assistance fund constitute the largest single item of veterans welfare 66968-9-367
Supply-Veterans Affairs services branch work load. Each case, on application or review, requires detailed information and careful appraisal, which is often quite time-consuming. The magnitude of this task is illustrated by the fact that during the past fiscal year 15,489 investigations and visits were made on behalf of new applicants for war veterans allowance, 44,627 for rechecks and 9,158 for assistance fund purposes.
This growing work load is consistent with the increase in recipients and expenditures of both the war veterans allowance and the assistance fund. In the past fiscal year a total of 14,055 recipients of war veterans allowance were helped by the assistance fund at a total cost of $2,095,521. In the previous fiscal year 11,819 were assisted at a cost of $1,448,278.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on the education assistance act. This is one aspect of our training program which continues to grow and is under the provisions of the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act. By March 31, 1959 the total approved for training had grown to 1,406 from 1,106 reported at March 31 of 1958. Total expenditures under this program from July 1, 1953 to March 31, 1959 were $1,156,340. Each case approved represents careful work in counselling the child concerned regarding the choice of career and follow-up on academic progress. The peak years of this program are still ahead of us, and it is impossible at this time to estimate exactly how long it will last.
This act was amended during the first session of the 24th parliament to provide that certain small classes of children previously unable to benefit from the provisions of this act should be eligible for assistance. The effect so far of the enlargement of the eligible classes has been small and only a dozen or so have been affected. However, the future should show an increasing effect from this amendment, although the total number of children who will eventually gain benefits is difficult to predict.
A further amendment provided for the increase in the permissible allowance from $25 to $60 a month for a number of eligible students between the ages of 21 and 25. So far 156 students have benefited from this increase, and the annual rate of allowance to them for the fiscal year just ended is about $33,000.
The Veterans Insurance Act was amended at the first session of the 24th parliament to extend the eligibility to contract for insurance for world war II veterans and those of the action in Korea to September 30, 1962. World war II veterans had lost eligibility to
5784	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs take out this insurance unless they had unused re-establishment credit available for premiums. Since the amendment some 2,727 policies have been issued for $10.3 million of insurance, of which we estimate nearly 2,000 gained their eligibility from the amendment, and the face amount of their policies is about $9 million.
The Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act and the Veterans Insurance Act were each amended to eliminate a restriction which had limited the face amount of insurance payable where a pension under the Pension Act was awarded to the dependant of a deceased pensioned policyholder. The effect of this amendment under the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act was slight because of the long period which has elapsed since the last of these policies was issued, in 1933. However, under the Veterans Insurance Act there have been some 223 death claims which have occurred since the amendment, representing a face value of about $643,800 which, on the basis of experience, would previously have been settled for approximately $450,600 but because of the amendment have become payable in full.
For the many years that I have been a member of this house I have known that the hospitals operated by our treatment services were generally held in high regard and that the work done in them was good. It was not, however, until I had the opportunity to visit them and see them with my own eyes that I realized just how good this work is.
It is on the clinical care of patients that the greatest public interest is focused. In this regard it is, of course, essential that proper drugs, equipment and buildings be available. I am happy to report that I have found our treatment services to be second to none in the supply of such adjuncts. Our equipment is in the main of the most modern type and is everywhere well maintained. An orderly program for the replacement of out-dated equipment ensures the continuance of this situation. Similarly, an orderly program for the replacement of outworn hospital buildings has been under way for some time and is still continuing. Another five or six years should see the disappearance of the old so-called "temporary" hospital accommodation and its replacement by modern fireproof buildings which should be worthy of the high quality of work carried out in them.
Construction work on the new wing at Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver, B.C., with a bed capacity of 314, has now reached approximately 40 per cent completion. It is expected to be ready for occupancy by April, 1960 and will replace beds and facilities in the old frame military hospital annex and in the Hycroft veterans home at Vancouver.


Planning is almost completed for the proposed new 300 bed wing at Westminster hospital, London, Ontario. It is expected that construction work will begin in the near future and will be completed in about two and a half years. Occupancy will permit the demolition of some of the older parts of the hospital dating from the first world war.
Planning is now under way for the addition of a veterans wing to the General hospital at St. John's, Newfoundland. This addition will provide for 35 active treatment beds and 30 beds for domiciliary care. It will also include an auditorium and offices as well as facilities for recreation and an arts and crafts program. It is hoped to start work on the project before the end of the present fiscal year and construction is expected to take about one year altogether.
The department has deliberately embarked upon a program to keep the practice of medicine in departmental hospitals a living, vital, progressive thing. We have allied ourselves as closely as we can to the teaching programs of universities, and we have been active in a program of clinical research in those fields of medicine which we are best suited, in view of the nature of our patient population, to investigate.
The members of this committee will want to know the extent to which this service can be extended to the veterans of Canada. It was never intended that everyone who had ever served in the armed forces of Canada in wartime would be provided with a free medical plan for the balance of his life. Such a concept would be an approach to state medicine, attended by whatever evils may be inherent in such a scheme, and would I fear alienate the good will of those of the medical profession to whom we are indebted. In any event, the department provides in its hospitals a grand total of 8,945 beds. When it is realized that there are now about 1,200,000 living Canadians who were once members of the armed forces, it will be obvious that the number of available beds is insufficient to serve all this large population.
It is the function of treatment services to make good the ravages of war. Thus the veterans who receive a pension for a service-connected disability are entitled to be admitted to one of our hospitals at any time for the necessary treatment of that disability. Similarly, the veteran who is a recipient of war veterans allowance may be admitted to a departmental hospital for any necessary treatment. Since he is dependent upon the department for food, clothing and shelter, it would be unreasonable not to provide him also with medical care.

In conclusion, with respect to the estimates which are before the committee, may I point out that in the administrative votes there is a substantial decrease of over $3 million. The group of expenditures which can be classified as payments under legislation or regulations and which total nearly $220 million of the department's total requirements of $307,285,000 is expected to show an increase in 19591960 of approximately $1,620,000. In the group of expenditures classed as "terminable services" the substantial increase in provision for the education of children of war dead is more than offset by the termination of unemployment insurance contributions by the department on behalf of discharged regular force personnel.
Mr. Chairman, we shall be going over my estimates item by item, and I shall be very pleased to answer any questions which hon. members may wish to ask.

speechtext:
We have just listened to an historically factual and comprehensive report by the Minister of Veterans Affairs with regard to the situation prevailing in his department as of this time. I suggest that the report which he has made to parliament be published in printed form and distributed throughout the country. It is something which is really worth having, and it has brought up to date the entire veterans charter.
I do not intend to waste the time of the committee by any lengthy dissertation on this matter. The main items of the estimates have been before the standing committee. The committee has been unanimous in its report. I do not think it is necessary to repeat today what was said there. However, observations will be made on each item, of course, as it is reached.
We all in the committee appreciate the value of the services of the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs, particularly those of the officials of the Veterans' Land Act administration and the Canadian pension commission. I think it may be truthfully said that at all times the committee has had at heart the interests of the veteran and his dependants.
A great many improvements have been made during the past few years in the legislation affecting veterans. There is one matter, however, which I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and which was not mentioned either in the committee or by him this morning. I refer to the question of small holdings under the Veterans' Land Act. In 1958, I think it was, the minister stated that he would make a careful investigation into this question of whether or not part-time holdings should not be reduced from 3 acres-or from 66968-9-367J
Supply-Veterans Affairs 1.6 acres which the figure actually is-to the original one half acre as it was in the beginning in 1945 or 1946. As far as my knowledge goes I am satisfied that the one half acre holding was a successful proposition in the section of the country from which I come. I would therefore ask the minister to review this situation, and possibly next year we shall be able to discuss the matter in committee.
I think that is all I have to say. As I say, we will discuss the estimates item by item as they come up.

Mr. Chairman, like the previous speaker I shall be quite brief, because we had a very thorough discussion of these estimates in the committee. I listened with interest to the historical review of the development of veterans affairs legislation and its present status. However, I do want to make a complaint. Everywhere I go I find that people pick on me. During the discussion of certain aspects of these estimates in the committee one of the officials, I think it was the deputy minister, was standing there reading over a document indicating that it was estimated that the first world war veteran would last until year so and so, and as soon as he told the committee that he looked at me. This morning the minister gave some information to the house with respect to the number of world war I veterans shrinking each year, and just at that point he looked at me. I want to protest about this, Mr. Chairman, and ask him in future to glance at someone else besides me. I am a bit sensitive in that respect.
I do want to take this opportunity briefly to express my appreciation for the courtesies the minister has extended and the prompt attention he has paid to any matter I have brought to his notice. I have no hesitation in saying of the minister that whether we get all we want from him we do know his heart is in the right place; what he has to do is persuade the rest of his colleagues that what he is asking for is justified. I would also like to express my appreciation to the deputy minister, the Canadian pension commission and the war veterans allowances board, as well as the senior officials in Ottawa, including the ladies, the district officials and the local officials. For a good number of years I have had a lot to do with the Department of Veterans Affairs, both as a member of the house and as one particularly interested in veterans questions. This is a department which has a devoted staff from top to bottom, working on behalf of the veterans and their dependants in Canada administering legislation passed by this house.
I might mention in passing that I received a telegram from the secretary of the civil

Supply-Veterans Affairs service branch representing the veterans employed in Shaughnessy hospital in Vancouver urging us to do all we could to prompt the government to grant the civil service increases which have been expected for some time. I want to take this opportunity to bring that to the minister's attention, because I think one of the best ways we can show our appreciation, particularly to the lower paid staff, is to urge the government to give the civil service increases which have been in mind and expected for so long.
The committee, I think, held ten meetings, made a thorough examination of the estimates and questioned the officials on all matters which required attention. There is no doubt that they have the information to give, or if they have not got it at the time they get it for you. We had representations from the Legion and a good number of veterans organizations on matters which are of particular concern to those groups. I might say that we heard representations with respect to the increase in pensions and war veterans allowances. The minister has no doubt noticed in the report the committee's reference to this, and we understand that consideration is being given to this matter at the present time and that legislation will be examined next year. I think a very good job was done in amending the Veterans' Land Act this year, and I believe it is a systematic way in approaching this legislation to deal with each particular act each year so we have it up to date for at least some time to come.
Then the committee heard some very interesting representations from the Hong Kong veterans and also some evidence from the officials concerned with that branch of veterans' affairs. I just want to read paragraph 18 on page 639 of the report in this connection:
The committee appreciates the difficulties of assuring an equitable distribution of the fund. At the same time it is aware of the special problems of veterans who were prisoners of war. It suggests that, in view of the obvious impossibility of settling all claims, the problem might be partially resolved by using a portion of the remaining balance to set up a prisoner of war benevolent fund to meet the human needs of prisoners of war and their dependants. This special fund could be administered after the fashion of similar benevolent funds already operating on behalf of veterans and their dependants.
The committee gave a lot of consideration to that and they have every sympathy with the recommendation that the Hong Kong veterans receive an increase in their allowance. We also had evidence with respect to the total of the fund and the claims against it, and we came to the unanimous
[Mr. Herridge.l
conclusion that this recommendation was possibly the best way to do the most for those who needed it the worst.
Then we had representations from the corps of Canadian fire fighters. I have always felt very sympathetic to their representations and their proposals, because I think the failure to recognize them is the result of some serious misunderstanding some years ago. In my opinion, from the evidence I listened to in the committee from time to time, there is some breach of faith on somebody's part. The committee suggested that as these measures are reviewed and amended from time to time consideration might be given to providing wider coverage to members of the corps as circumstances warrant. This applies particularly to the war veterans allowance as the corps members reach age eligibility.
I do urge the minister to give consideration to that recommendation of the committee. There again, they are few in numbers to commence with. Age is, of course, taking its toll, and possibly we can do something to the best advantage along the lines recommended by the committee.
Then the committee heard some representations with respect to the veterans preference regarding employment in the civil service. There has been some uncertainty in certain quarters, and to clear up any uncertainty there might be on this point the committee heartily endorsed the principle of the veterans principle in the Civil Service Act, and recommended that in any contemplated amendment of the act this principle remain unchanged.
I think it is safe to say from experience that the work of the standing committee is justified. I think we can look upon the standing committee on veterans affairs as a clearing house through which representatives of veterans organizations can advance their complaints, make their suggestions and express their opinions, and discuss things generally of interest to veterans and their dependants with the members of the committee.
I have just two other matters to mention before I resume my seat, Mr. Chairman. First of all, I do want to support the representations made by the hon. member for Renfrew North with respect to further consideration being given to the reduction of the required acreage with regard to small holdings to half an acre. If only we could get that acreage reduced to half an acre I am sure there would be thousands of veterans in Canada who would take advantage of that splendid legislation. As I have said on a number of occasions, in my constituency I

am quite positive that there would be between 200 and 300 applications from veterans who are employed by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, the lumber industry, or in the mining industry in the district who would like an opportunity to obtain half an acre of land under the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act in order to build a home.
We do urge further consideration of that matter. In a mountainous country like ours it is most difficult even to get the 1.6 acres on occasion, and anywhere near our cities and towns it is almost impossible to get 3 acres. Naturally our town and villages are on the side of streams and face the large mountains. That leaves little room for this purpose.
I listened carefully to what the minister said about the admission of veterans to hospital for treatment, and I agree that it was not intended that this should develop into a state medical scheme for all veterans. At the recent convention of the British Columbia command of the Canadian Legion this was discussed, and I received letters from a number of branches. We raise more hell in British Columbia than in any other province. Even the Canadian Legion feels that way about us. We are that way in all respects. We are possibly the most progressive province in Canada.
Before registering my complaint in mild language, because I do not wish to be nasty, I want to read a letter I received from an old sergeant in my company which indicates that the vast majority of veterans appreciate what is being done for them by the Department of Veterans Affairs:
Nakusp, May 1, 1959
Friend Bert:
Just a line to thank you for all your favors. It is very interesting to know what goes on down there, although I am unable to read a great deal owing to defective eyes.
I have just written the D.V.A. at Vancouver. I felt that I must let them know that I appreciated what they have done for me.
After my wife died last April with eight years of medical and surgical expenses, it had left me broke and when the $90 per month came in so unexpectedly, it was such a surprise that I have not really recovered from it yet.
And I have to also thank you people down there. I fully realize that thanks sounds very weak and inadequate, but it is all I can think of at the present time. And so again I say thank you all for a very wonderful lift.
Very sincerely,
J. S. Crowell
Trust your health continues good.
Anyone who says anything against the D.V.A. will have to fight me.
I receive many letters of that type. I put this one on the record because it may give
Supply-Veterans Affairs a feeling of satisfaction to the officials and everyone connected with the administration of veterans affairs. On one occasion when I was admitted to Shaughnessy hospital for treatment a neighbouring bed patient asked if I had spent five years in the New Westminster penitentiary. When I replied that up to that point I had not, he told me I resembled the chap in the cell next to him. He had been in trouble and told me all his difficulties.
I have had a number of cases referred to me of destitute veterans who were not eligible, according to law, to be admitted to hospital. I received a letter from a member of the provincial executive of the Canadian Legion in British Columbia who informed me that there were 52 empty beds when they went through the hospital. These cases arise particularly in respect of world war I veterans. With that equipment and plant available I urge that we do not fail to admit to hospital any veteran who has worn the uniform of this country in world war I or world war II. I urge that consideration be given particularly to these older men who seek admission to our departmental hospitals.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to endorse the last statement made by the previous speaker, and also a couple of the other statements he made during the course of his remarks. In rising at this time I assure the committee that I do not wish to take up too much time. I shall briefly present my three points and express the hope that by one o'clock the minister's responsibilities here will be completed.
None of us in any way suggests that our veterans legislation is not among the best, but as is the case in all legislation there are inequities, and I wish to refer to some existing inequities in our pension legislation. Although these points were discussed at length in the standing committee I wish to bring them to the attention of this committee for an express purpose.
The previous speaker referred to the fund that exists in the department of the Secretary of State due to the fact that assets of enemy countries were seized by the Canadian government at the beginning of world war II. He suggested, as did the veterans affairs committee, that this money be used to establish a fund to take care of certain contingencies that arise and for which no provision is made under any existing legislation.
I mention this point because of a number of cases that have been brought to my personal attention. Having been a prisoner during world war II and being now a member of this committee, no doubt certain cases

Supply-Veterans Affairs are brought to my attention which may not have come to the notice of other hon. members.
Cases have been referred to me of comrades of mine who passed away at an early age leaving young wives and very young families. As was my own experience, these men were invariably discharged from the services with a small medical pension. In their particular cases they did not follow up with any great degree of enthusiasm the infirmity they had at the time of discharge. Suddenly one day these men did not return to their homes and families; in each case they died suddenly. Because of their desire to be good citizens and achieve independence there was no means by which their families could be supported following their death.
A couple of these cases were in the Toronto area and I was able to acquaint myself intimately with the circumstances. I told the standing committee of a case involving a young widow who upon the death of her husband applied to the department and was rejected under the terms of the act because her veteran husband was not in receipt of a 50 per cent medical pension. She then applied to the provincial welfare authorities. Because the veteran had been industrious, had worked hard and built up a small estate which under the terms of his will provided her with a small monthly return, she was refused support by the provincial authorities.
Here we have the case of this young widow-as a matter of fact it applies to all the cases I know of-these young widows, having a small income on a reduced basis per year for a short time, possibly 10 years, with young families and existing-and I say "existing"-on less than the mothers' allowances in the province of Ontario. I consider this a very poor situation in regard to the widows and families of those veterans.
Mr. Chairman, inasmuch as the Pension Act is to be reviewed next year, these situations should be taken into serious consideration. When the act is amended I shall certainly be active in the standing committee to see that these situations are rectified. I feel very badly about them myself as a member of parliament, and I feel considerably worse because of the fact that these men were comrades of mine. If it were brought to the attention of the country I am sure the country would also feel as I do about these cases.
The previous speaker referred to the sum of money that is under the control of the Secretary of State as the result of confiscating enemy assets in Canada. This morning we heard the Minister of Finance say that sum is not as large as the amount quoted in

the standing committee, which was something over $6 million; in actual fact it is $4 milion. I do not think the Minister of Finance informed us that the claims against this fund are in excess of $100 million, but some of those claims are by large corporations which were warned in plenty of time to get out of those countries at the beginning of the second world war, and they had the opportunity to save their assets but did not pay heed. I do not suggest for a moment that this money be taken as is or that the whole amount be used, because I suppose there are many just cases that must be considered. But if there is a residual amount, then I think the action suggested by the hon. member for Kootenay West should be considered and taken under advisement by the minister and his department in the future.
Finally I should like to say a word about Sunnybrook hospital in Toronto. I suppose these conditions may exist in other veterans hospitals as well. There is a terrific increase in the number of aged veterans being taken into the hospital under domiciliary care. Since they have been taken into Sunnybrook the strain has been on active treatment beds. I believe the minister should consider the need for active treatment beds in relation, of course, to the demand; and we know and the members of the standing committee know that it is quite considerable.
I think all the members felt as I felt on viewing the situation. Because of the fact that these aged veterans are being properly cared for-and the treatment they receive is commendable-we feel that the administrative areas are being sacrificed. Certain office space, and certainly the admitting and other facilities, are being taxed to supply this domiciliary care. We also noted that the area which is used at Sunnybrook for ambulance cases is very poor, very inadequate and certainly in the cold winter months presents many difficulties. It is because of this situation that I mention Sunnybrook at this time. I hope the minister will use his influence to see that next year there will be an item in the estimates to take care of this situation and see that it is rectified for the veterans using that particular institution.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with others who have spoken in thanking the minister for the comprehensive review of his department which he gave us this morning. In particular I should like to thank him for the information he gave us on the treatment facilities and the new hospital facilities which are being provided for Newfoundland veterans, and the good news that they should be completed in about a year from now.

When the main estimates were first presented I was surprised to find a decrease of about $1,727,000, but I note that when the supplementary estimates are added, if my arithmetic is correct, the over-all total shows a slight increase of about $70,000. I draw attention to this fact because I think hon. members and the committee should not conclude from these figures that the estimates of this department are being stabilized or that they can be stabilized in the near future. There are several forces at work which directly affect the estimates of this department. One of the factors is the rates and scales of allowances and pensions. As the purchasing power of our dollar continues to decline these rates and scales will have to be revised upward from time to time to enable the veteran to keep abreast of the increase in the cost of living.
The other main factor has to do with the number of veterans for whom benefits must be provided. The minister informed us this morning that the number of veterans of world war I has passed its peak and that the payments to veterans of world war II can be expected to increase; but as the years advance and more and more of the old sweats answer the last roll call, payments to this group will continue to decline and eventually disappear.
In addition to the two factors I have already mentioned there are three others which, though less spectacular in their effect on the budget, are nevertheless very important. As time goes on the effect of advancing years must tend to aggravate the war disabilities of the veterans of world war II and render them eligible for increased pensions and disability grants. The inexorable march of time will inevitably render more and more of world war II veterans eligible for war veterans allowances. These payments are now limited by a means test; but, due to inflation, the ceiling has been raised from time to time and it must be expected that this will happen again in the future.
Another factor, and a more important one, is that benefits should be extended to certain groups of veterans who are not eligible at present. In addition, as Canada advances in prosperity we shall have to raise these ceilings to enable the veteran to share in the improved standard of living enjoyed by Canadians generally. For all these reasons, then, it is reasonable to expect an increase in the estimates of this department for many years to come. In fact the only way these increases can be held in check is by the stabilization of the purchasing power of our dollar and by continued prosperity which will enable the means test to come into effect even
Supply-Veterans Affairs when the ceiling is raised to provide for improvement in living standards.
In spite of all that has been done under the veterans charter there is still need for further machinery to take care of those veterans under 60 whose earning capacity has been destroyed by ill health for long periods of time, and who cannot qualify for benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act because their disabilities are not attributable to war service or because even when their disabilities are attributable to war service they cannot be certified by a medical doctor as being permanently unemployable. These veterans have no recourse but to apply for public relief.

I thank the minister for that correction. I was aware of that, but the group I have in mind are those under 60 whose disabilities are not attributable to war service and who lose their earning capacity for long periods of time. These veterans have no recourse but to apply for public relief, and to me it seems a national disgrace that any person who offered his life for his country should have to rely on public charity in a time of personal misfortune.
We have a duty to keep before the public the fact that the prosperity and privileges we enjoy every day have been made possible by the sacrifices of our comrades who gave their all, and also by the services of those who offered their lives but were fortunate enough to survive. It is easy even for veterans to forget this fact. This was vividly brought home to me personally when along with other members of the committee I visited Sunnybrook hospital at Toronto. We were impressed not only with the multitude of activities carried on in that institution, which can almost be described as a self-contained community, but once more we were reminded anew of the horrors of war, which had become dimmed by the passage of time. There we saw living reminders of the human cost of war and living testimony to the price some of our comrades have continued to pay throughout the years.
This experience of being confronted with the grim reality of the price some of our comrades are still paying came to me as a bit of a shock, though I knew from experience

Supply-Veterans Affairs what to expect. In my opinion it is an experience that should be made available to every member of the house, to high school and university students and to as many of the adult public as can be conveniently accommodated. I hope the minister will consider this suggestion, because to me it is essential lest we forget.
When the committee was considering the first item of these estimates representations were received from several veterans organizations which in my opinion are worthy of serious study. As most of these representations involved the expenditure of public funds the committee could not make specific recommendations. However, I hope the minister and his colleagues will find it possible to give them the sympathetic and favourable consideration which in my opinion they deserve.
The corps of Canadian fire fighters in particular requested greater recognition of their valuable war service. Their request appears to me to be fully justified, and I hope the minister will find some way of overcoming the technicalities which now cause them to be classed as civilians instead of veterans. Such a change will not result in any significant expenditure of public funds.
Finally, as a representative from Newfoundland I was happy to have the minister's assurance that the Pension Act will be revised at the next session of parliament. I know I am voicing the sentiments of all Newfoundlanders when I say we hope that at that time the necessary changes will be made to put Newfoundland veterans completely on a par with those who served in the Canadian forces, in accordance with the commitment contained in the terms of union.
As other hon. members have pointed out, these estimates were thoroughly examined in the standing committee on veterans affairs. Every item was gone over with a fine-tooth comb and there was also an inquiry into the operation of the various branches. I am sure all members of the committee were impressed, as I was, with the competence of the officials in charge of the administration of the veterans charter and were thoroughly satisfied that all these funds are being administered with competence and efficiency.
All members in all parties are one in their desire to give the best possible treatment to our war veterans, and I am sure there is nothing controversial on that score either with respect to policy or the individual items in the estimates. Therefore I agree with hon. members that it should not be necessary for the committee to take very much time in passing these estimates.

Mr. Chairman, at this time I should like to make a few brief comments on "veterans preference." I know that one or two previous speakers have also referred to this subject, but I should like to take this opportunity to refer to the matter because at this time there is some suggestion that in the revamping of the civil service commission there might be a change in the handling of applications through that body. This matter is of concern, in my humble opinion, to a large number of veterans and,
I	might say, to many Canadian citizens who realize and appreciate the great sacrifices that have been made by veterans for their country, who feel that no change should be made at the present time.
In that connection, I should like to refer to the brief I have here, a copy of which was presented to the standing committee on veterans affairs by the Canadian Legion in March of this year. Under the heading "Civil Service" and the subheading, "Maintenance of Preference", I quote the following:
The federal Civil Service Act is presently under review and it is anticipated that amendments to the act may result. We believe Canada has benefited by the veterans preference in that it tends to ensure that a high percentage of civil servants will be veterans who have already demonstrated their loyalty by their willingness to make great sacrifices in defence of this country. The Canadian Legion is strongly opposed to any amendment to this act which would take away any benefit presently accruing to Canadian veterans.
The Canadian Legion therefore recommends-that the existing veterans preference in employment in the civil service be maintained and applied to all government departments and crown corporations.
I think it is generally known, Mr. Chairman, that the veterans preference has been in effect since world war I. This principle was firmly recognized when it was made statutory and included in the early stages of planning for the rehabilitation of veterans of world war II. I might say that within three months of the beginning of world war
II	a special committee of the cabinet was set up to deal with the rehabilitation of veterans, under which there was set up a general advisory committee of deputy ministers which spelled out a program of rehabilitation in answer to this question: "What does the state owe to those whose peaceful lives were disrupted by service to this country." Mr. Walter S. Woods, C.M.G., Ll.D., former deputy minister of veterans affairs, had a great deal to do with drawing up the veterans charter. I should mention also the role played by the Canadian Legion in formulating that charter. It was a most important and substantial one.

Mr. Woods, in his splendid book "The Men Who Came Back", refers to the general principles on pages 128 and 129, and I should like to read the 12th principle of the program. No. 12 reads:
They should be given preference in the civil service similar to that extended to veterans of world war X.
This principle, of course, Mr. Chairman, only applies when the veteran concerned has passed the regular civil service examinations, so I think what is being asked is certainly not unfair or unreasonable. This system, since it has been in effect, I submit has worked out very well, and many of our best civil servants are veterans. It is natural, perhaps, to expect that those who have shown the highest form of unselfish service to their country should prove later to be the highest type of civil servant the government could hire.
I might point out that one of our veterans affairs subdepartments, the Veterans' Land Act branch, has been held up on many occasions as a model of good organization and efficient administration. The system of veterans preference has proven fair, and I think there is no justification at the present time for changing it. There are, of course, not many veterans who apply in a number of the competitions, and in quite a large number of competitions there are none who apply. There are still some however who are entitled to the privilege of veterans preference due to their service, and especially some veterans of the Korean war, who must be given consideration.
I might say that most private companies, municipalities and provincial governments recognize the principle of veterans preference in their hiring. Certainly the federal civil service should lead the way and continue the good example that has been set. The legislation in this regard has been on the books for a good many years, and I repeat that I do not see any reason for changing it at the present time.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that this subject is not particularly the responsibility of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I only raise it at the present time because the department has a vital interest in everything connected with the veterans, so I think it is not inopportune. I might close by saying that this subject is causing a great deal of concern amongst veterans, the organizations to which they belong, and many citizens throughout the country who are interested in veterans. I hope no changes will be made.

They should first be remembered by the government and the parliament of Canada.
I should like to put on the record some figures with respect to the Canadians who in four wars, in the 60 years of this century, have laid down their lives for their country. In the South African war 224 Canadians gave their lives. In world war I 60,969 Canadians gave their lives. In world war II 42,042 Canadians gave their lives. In the Korean war 312 Canadians laid down their lives in far lands but in the defence of the world and of Canada particularly.
I think it is the responsibility of the parliament of Canada to mark the day of remembrance of our war dead so that future generations will remember that 103,547 Canadians have given their lives for their country in the defence and maintenance of the freedom we enjoy. I strongly urge that the minister use his good offices with his colleagues in the cabinet to have Remembrance day made a statutory holiday and that the government -and the Department of Veterans Affairs particularly-make it a point that this day of remembrance of our war dead be honoured as much as possible all over Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take just a few minutes of the time of the committe since I did not have the opportunity to be a member of the standing committee which studied the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I have just a few remarks to make which concern the veterans in my area in northwestern Quebec. I want to stress one point which has already been brought to the attention of the minister and the officials of his department, but since I have received an additional representation from the Canadian Legion, at Amos and Senneterre in my riding and other legions in

the district, I feel it is my duty to bring this question to the attention of the minister.
The matter concerns the veterans in our area. We have an area covering practically 100,000 square miles and taking in the northern part of Pontiac-Temiscamingue riding, the riding of Villeneuve next to mine and my riding of Chapleau. Throughout this large territory there are some 6,000 veterans. We have at Amos an office to look after the Veterans' Land Act administration. A representative has been in charge there for a number of years, although last year there was a change; a new officer was appointed, but the office was maintained. However, this man is alone and he is expected to do the whole job and cover this large area. He also has to look after the welfare of the different veterans in this territory.
This is almost an impossible job for one man to do. I believe we require a welfare officer as well as the representative of the department who looks after the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. Hence with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should just like to read into the record a resolution that was adopted last year by all the Canadian Legion branches in northwestern Quebec at the meeting held in Amos. Since this resolution is in French I will read it in French. (Translation):
Mr. Chairman, as I have just explained, in northwestern Quebec there is a vast area to cover. It is almost 100,000 square miles and the population includes 6,000 veterans who do not get all the attention they would have a right to expect from the Department of Veterans Affairs, not because of the department's unwillingness to give them attention but because those veterans are scattered over such a vast area that it is impossible for the department to do so with only one representative. It might seem like a small number of veterans compared with the number of those around Montreal or Toronto, who do get more attention paid to them. However, there surely can be no doubt as to their patriotism, and even if they are spread out on a vast area, they are just as entitled to the attention of the department as are veterans who live in towns and cities.
I should like to read into the record the text of a resolution on this matter adopted last year on the occasion of the annual rally of northwestern Quebec Canadian Legion branches held in Amos on August 3, 1958:
From the veterans of northwestern Quebec to the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Whereas the northwest area of the province of Quebec, comprising the federal ridings of Chapleau, Villeneuve and part of Pontiac, includes over six thousand (6,000) veterans, nearly half of whom

have to do with the Department of Veterans Affairs; Whereas the only federal agency in the area is the Veterans Land Act Board, represented by a single member who also has to perform the duties of a welfare officer; Whereas the official holding both the above-mentioned offices without any help whatsoever, at the present time, in the form of an assistant, a secretary, or other persons, is finding it impossible to perform the administrative work required of him, to the satisfaction of the department and of the veterans concerned; Whereas the Val d'Or, Senneterre, Malartic and Amos branches of the Canadian Legion, after considering the matter, have come to the conclusion that this situation is mainly due to the overburdensome cumulation of two administrative offices each of which should be assigned to a separate official, to wit, an official for the Veterans' Land Act Administration and an official for the Veterans Welfare Services, with due regard for and appreciation of the work done in the cities of Val d'Or and Rouyn-Noranda by two officials of the Unemployment Insurance Commission who are allowed by the Department of Labour to give over to this work ten per cent of their office time by virtue of an agreement with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Be it therefore proposed, resolved and unanimously carried: That it be recommended to federal authorities to improve the administration of the affairs of northwest Quebec veterans by the establishment of two administrative positions with administrative jurisdiction over our area:
(a)	one representative from the Department of Veterans Affairs, Welfare Services Division;
(b)	one representative from the Veterans' Land Act Administration.
And the document is signed by:
W. A. Abbott, District commanding officer.
P. H. Poitras, District secretary.
Canadian Legion, North-West district of the province of Quebec.
As I said, a representative of the veterans land act board, a new man, has been put in charge of the office in Amos, and has now taken up his duties. But the man cannot handle all the work by himself, and that is why I thought I should bring this matter to the attention of the minister when the estimates of the veterans affairs department are before the house.

Mr. Chairman, on this item I just want to renew the plea which the 

minister receives annually, I think, from veterans. There is need for greater care in granting the veteran the benefit of the doubt. In recent years more and more cases have come to my attention in which the veteran has not received the benefit of the doubt. I should like to take a moment or two to cite a few examples.
I know of the case of a veteran who was accepted into the navy with a lame leg. After a number of years of service he was discharged. He did not apply for pension, but after having been in civilian life for a number of years the leg became worse. Being a veteran he applied for a pension. The board decided that it was a pre-enlistment disability not aggravated by his service in the navy, so he did not receive any pension. This man cannot now earn a living to support his family and has to live on public charity.
With all due respect to medical opinion I find it difficult to believe-and I regard myself as a reasonable person-that a lame person could go into the navy and serve for two or three years without aggravating his infirmity but the minute he engages in a civilian occupation his condition immediately begins to get worse. This does not seem to me a reasonable stand.
I have another case of a veteran who was taken into the service with defective sight. In North Africa it got worse and he had to be discharged. He applied for a pension and was told his disability was pre-enlistment, not aggravated by his service, and he was denied a pension. It seems to me there is something wrong somewhere. Perhaps the doctors who assess these cases are not aware of the need to give the veteran the benefit of the doubt. It appears that if they can find a loophole at all they use it to give the benefit of doubt to the department. A veteran may have a nervous breakdown or some nervous disorder five, six or even ten years after discharge. Who can say that his service did not contribute to the breakdown? I believe there is a need for greater care to be taken in giving the benefit of the doubt to veterans who apply for pensions.

In reply to the hon. member let me say this. In the case of the veteran who came into the navy with a disability, which case the hon. member cited, I take-it that the medical history during the man's service indicated that his condition was not aggravated by his service. Some years after he left the service it did become aggravated. The hon. member can appreciate that these cases are very difficult. I was a member of the standing committee on veterans affairs for a number of years, and I recall that the question of benefit of doubt was considered

by many committees. We attempted to introduce a section in the legislation which we thought would cover all this problem.
I have looked through many files on such cases. If hon. members could see these files and appreciate how these matters are studied and restudied they would agree, as I had to agree myself, that the benefit of the doubt was given to the veteran in 99 cases out of 100. It is a question sometimes of whose doubt it is. As far as the act is concerned it must be the doubt of the board and the experienced and competent men who serve on it.
I frankly do not see how the act could be improved very much, but we would appreciate it if the hon. member and any other hon. members in this committee would refer to us individual cases which come to their attention. If we can assist in any way we will.
