maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to make a report on the progress of the national development program. Up to this time there has been no coherent account of the program on Hansard, and I should like to do what I can to try to get it in perspective.
In the first place, the national development program covers several departments. Under the act that serves as a guide to the operation of my department there is a clear directive to formulate resource development and conservation plans in co-operation with other departments, provincial and municipal governments and private interests. Therefore I will take the liberty of mentioning aspects of the development plan which come under other departments as well as my own.
The departments of agriculture and trade and commerce have made a good start on the basic cornerstone of the development policy by embarking on the implementation of a national agricultural policy. Cash advances, the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act, the crop insurance legislation, the farm credit legislation, are important items in the field of statute law to start a fundamental revision of agricultural policies in Canada. Increasing sales of wheat, box car allotment, grain demurrage charges, an investigation into the spread of prices between producer and consumer and import controls on farm products are examples of the aggressive attitude of this government toward problems that have faced agriculture for some time. We recognize that without a sound agricultural industry there is no foundation on which to build a larger and more prosperous nation.
The national development program has as its ultimate aim the increased processing of our tremendous natural resources, using the increasing reserves of various forms of


energy available in Canada. It was no accident that the first move of the new government when it met parliament in October, 1957 was to announce a royal commission on energy. I am proud to sit in the present parliament which passed the national energy board act and put into effect the main recommendations of the royal commission. It gives to us responsibility for planning the first ingredient for a national energy policy, namely a board that will keep a rolling inventory of our energy resources and advise the government on the best use of all our energy resources in the national interest.
The development program falls into three main divisions in so far as the first stages of the plan are concerned. These are first, delineation of resources; second, power; and third, conservation. The delineation part of the program is going well. The purpose of this part of the plan is to open up Canada for exploration and development. We must find out what we have, where it is and how much we have of each type of renewable and nonrenewable resources. Good work has been done over the years on the forest inventory program, water power, fish resources and wild life, while very little is known of a great proportion of our country horizontally, and even less vertically. Obviously the first need in a development plan is to have ready access to this information. The means used to achieve this are roads, air fields, water and sea transport, railroads where economic, and the concomitant necessities of research of all kinds, radio, radar, weather stations, and so forth.
The roads to resources program has aroused a good deal of interest. The Prime Minister announced on February 12, 1958 that there would be approximately a $100 million road program in the Territories and Yukon in the next seven years. I have made it clear that economics would play a large part in setting the priorities of the proposed parts of this grid system through the potentially wealthy parts of northern Canada. For instance, the level of activity of oil and gas exploration in the northern Yukon and the lower Mackenzie valley makes it mandatory that we push forward the road from Flat Creek to a terminal on the Arctic coast or Mackenzie estuary as rapidly as engineering and efficient operation allow us to move.
On the other hand, the balance of interest along the planned route to Great Bear lake from Great Slave lake seems to be less than the interest in the mineral resources around Great Slave lake. Therefore we are now considering shifting our survey crews to the Yellowknife-Fort Reliance road. The same sort of economic criteria are applied to each

road. Within the over-all framework of the government's development policy an interdepartmental committee advises me on the choice of routes and sets the priorities for construction. The engineers of public works advise me on the standards, call for tenders and supervise construction.
There is little value in having a grid system of roads in the new territories, Mr. Chairman, to open up new petroleum and mineral areas in the territories unless there are roads or railroads or waterways to tie up to the settled areas to the south. Therefore the second aspect of the roads to resources program is a series of co-operative agreements with the provinces. We have offered to pay one half the cost of roads in the provinces that will open up new resource areas. At the present time nine provinces are working on such roads. One provincial agreement has been signed with the province of British Columbia, and I hope the final polishing up of the terms will permit the working agreements to be put into written form at an early date. The federal government has agreed to pay one half the cost up to $1,500,000 per year to a total of one half of a total of $15 million for each province over a period of years that is mutually satisfactory.
Under the roads to resources program some 2,000 miles of road are planned for the Territories and Yukon, and over 4,000 miles in the provinces. I believe the people of Canada will agree with me when I say that this program is imaginative and has been carefully planned. It gives to Canadians the satisfaction that the government is actively carrying out the people's expressed wish to open up their country for exploration and development.
In addition to roads, other means of access must be improved. The committee has already heard of the plans to take over the air fields in northern Canada associated with the D.E.W. line. This will be a two or three year operation and will make it much easier for private exploration teams to move freely in our far northern regions. This operation is being carried out mainly by the Department of Transport. In addition to these air fields, other air strips are being considered, weather reporting services are being improved and navigational aids are being provided and improved.
The Department of Transport is engaged in getting know-how on large scale resupply operations in the Arctic. Last year the western portion of the D.E.W. line was supplied by the Department of Transport. This year they will resupply all D.E.W. line stations. Increased tonnages generally are being moved with greater confidence. My personal compliments go to the men of the marine division
Supply-Northern Affairs of the Department of Transport, the men who plan the operations, those who operate the icebreakers and the supply ships. In addition, one private enterprise company with tug and barges moved from Vancouver to Spence bay and back last summer. If this deed had been done five years ago it would have been called an international saga of the northern seas, but now it is becoming just a routine operation.
Another part of the department's operations that deals with delineation of resources is the winter work program of co-operation with the provinces in building forest access roads. Under this eight months a year program the federal government pays 50 per cent of the cost. Provincial officials tell me that this is one of the most appreciated programs of the government.
The total estimated cost to the federal government of the road program to open up resources during this first stage of development is about $200 million. I cannot accurately estimate at this time the cost of the other parts of the delineation program. In view of the tremendous activity already generated in oil and gas exploration and the even greater activity that I expect in the mineral field, I suggest that this part of the program will be regarded in years to come as having been responsible for one of the major surges forward in the opening up of our country. Possibly it will be comparable to the building of the C.P.R.
The second part of the development program deals with power. Any person who examines the resources of Canada soon becomes aware of the importance of power. Power is not just obtained from water resources. The best thinking now is clear that the largest amount of power at the lowest price comes from a combination of thermal power and hydro power. The thermal power to provide the base load can be produced from coal, uranium, natural gas, oil, butane or propane, depending on the presence of these energy fuels. The power from water can best be used for peaking purposes.
Therefore in planning for the best use of our energy resources we will have to assess the ability of a region to supply the necessary power. Applying that reasoning to the Atlantic provinces, the house can appreciate why I asked the premiers of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to allow me to include Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland in the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act. It explains why the federal government offered to build transmission lines in Newfoundland emanating from Bay d'Espoir. To us it seems elementary that we should encourage transmission lines in those eastern provinces in the expectation

Supply-Northern Affairs that eventually there will be a grid system covering the whole Atlantic area. In that way the coal of the Atlantic provinces can be tied in with the hydro power of the Saint John, the Passamaquoddy and the Hamilton rivers.
There are those who scoff, Mr. Chairman, at thinking ahead like this, but my answer is that not only is this the only course to follow, but when I see these older provinces by the sea trying so hard to help themselves I know that this government will not fail them by being frightened of a little ridicule by making known its long range plans.
The provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan are also showing a laudable desire to work together by joining their transmission lines. The whole Nelson-Saskatchewan-Churchill system will have to be examined to plan for the eventual full utilization of the hydro power in this area. Fortunately the prairies have large quantities of fossil fuels to integrate with their hydro. Ontario and Manitoba co-operate closely, as do Quebec and Ontario, in the interchanging of power.
Probably of most interest to the committee is present progress on the Columbia river. A year ago we were still awaiting relevant engineering reports. Last fall, after a full study of both the engineering and economic aspects of the Columbia river system, we decided to enter into a co-operative effort with the United States to use fully this great water resource on condition that the United States government agreed to a fair division of the downstream benefits. A great forward step was taken when the government of the United States agreed to negotiate with us on this basis. Once these two key decisions were taken we immediately set up a joint policy committee of the dominion government and the government of British Columbia. This liaison committee is composed of two dominion ministers, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself, two British Columbia ministers and technical staffs from both governments.
Meanwhile the international joint commission is working out the complex problem of deciding what the downstream power benefits and flood control benefits amount to and what system of division should be adopted. The international joint commission meets almost every month. A close liaison is maintained between the joint policy committee and the international joint commission.
It is my opinion that success will attend all these efforts. In the first place, both countries know that by co-operation both nations can receive more units of power at a lower price. Second, all parties know there has to be a fair deal for both countries. Because of

our common democratic procedures, any decision will have to be ratified by the United States Senate, and it must be satisfied that their country benefits from the arrangement. In Canada the decision will have to be approved by the legislature of British Columbia and the parliament of Canada. We certainly will want to assure ourselves that a full share of the downstream benefits created by Canadian storage will be paid to British Columbia in the form of power.
I detect a great desire on both sides of the border to push this great project to a conclusion. When one realizes that the power at stake is several times the amount produced at the new St. Lawrence seaway dam at Cornwall, one can appreciate the tremendous importance of this deal to the northwestern United States and British Columbia.
Once again, with respect to development on the Columbia river we visualize the multiple use of resources. The strategic coal reserves of British Columbia and Alberta will fit in very nicely with these vast hydro resources to provide more and more of the base load power for the eastern end of the transmission grids. It is no accident that the new energy bill contained a clause allowing for 25-year export licences for electricity. I have every expectation that the present small boom in the coal mining industry of the Crowsnest region will spread to other parts of the coal areas.
In addition to the above developments, we are continuing studies of the Saint John river, the Fraser river, the Yukon river and the Fort Smith area, and soon I should like to organize a study of the Nelson and Churchill river systems.
Thus it can be seen that our development policy is moving steadily forward on building up the basic regional ingredients of a national power policy. This policy will include all forms of energy, and explains how urgent a national energy board is to our plans. To be able to proceed economically with regional power grids we have called in provincial power commissions, private power companies, electrical equipment companies, to join with our research agencies in a co-ordinated attack on the problem of long-range transmission of electric power.
By increasing our knowledge of raw materials and our energy resources we will be better able to reach the ultimate goal of greater processing in Canada to provide for a bigger and better Canada. The vision of a nation on the northern half of this continent moving toward its destiny is not just a dream. It is a realistic effort of many dedicated people who have been brought out of backwaters to help implement a new, positive conception of the role of government.

In this whole program there are no more dedicated people than those in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. This department is the eyes and ears of my department. It is no fault of theirs that 55 per cent of Canada remained unmapped, nor that it would have taken 250 years more to complete the necessary hydrographic surveys of our coastal waters. It gives me great pleasure to say how happy I am that this government has agreed to plan to double the hydrographic service and the geological service in the next five years. All Canadians will be proud that a Canadian scientific expedition is now operating, and will operate every year in our Arctic islands to give us basic information so desperately needed for our development program. The metallurgical division of that department has been examined and found equal to the tasks that are before them. I fully believe that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is completely aware of the part they must play in the development program. I feel that they will meet the challenge. I want to express my personal appreciation of the efforts their members have made to give my department the information we require.
The third part of the development program deals with conservation. In my personal opinion, and I hope of others, this is perhaps the most important part of the national development program. This is a concept of the multiple use of resources. This is a concept of co-operation with the provinces, with conservation boards, with private organizations and with individuals and universities. A start has been made. All the provinces met with the dominion government last November. The decision was made to hold a full scale conference in 1960 to deal with renewable resources. In the meantime the provinces have submitted reports on what they are doing and what gaps exist. We are providing the secretariat to work under a joint dominion-provincial steering committee. A great deal has to be done this summer and fall in the preparation of the basic material for the conference.
The needs of various regions differ, but I am sure that we can decide on the principles under which the various governments and agencies can operate. We must succeed in getting all groups to commit themselves to a positive program of using our resources to the best advantage for the future of the people of Canada. There are many things such as northern research, the national parks, historic sites, wildlife, in my department that play an important part in the over-all development plan. There is the atomic energy
Supply-Northern Affairs program which plays a key role in that program. I could, if I had more time, give you some idea of my plans as to how the national development program will bear upon our centennial celebrations. But I believe I have said enough to indicate that there is a coherent working out of the blueprints and that the vision is shining brighter every month.
I should like to add a few sentences on human resources. A few months ago Maclean's magazine published one of the most moving accounts of human thought and endurance that I have ever read. It was written by Farley Mowat. I recommend to every member of the house and every Canadian the readings of this story. Here, in clear and powerful prose, an attempt is made to look into the minds of people thousands of years removed from us in civilization. Read that story and you will understand why my department, and this government, is not going to overlook the tremendous assets and personal needs of these old and long-overlooked Canadian citizens. We cannot take unto ourselves the smugness that we will always be right in our dealings with these first Canadians. We know that they are human beings who have a great need and a great potential. This government, to the limit of its knowledge will not fail our Eskimo people.
Last year, for the first time in over a quarter of a century, my department appeared before the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. It appeared before that committee again this year and, as hon. members know, a very forthright report was tabled in this house a few days ago. Officials in my department who appeared before that committee were told to express themselves freely and without reservation. The members of the committee recognized this, I believe, and were very searching and forthright in their questioning. Their report makes many worthwhile observations and recommendations which deserve, and are now receiving, full consideration by my department. I can assure hon. members that I welcome the vigorous approach the standing committee took in its examination of my department. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that my officials are now taking an equally vigorous approach in their examination of the observations and recommendations.
I believe that Canadians generally support northern development, and that they understand that costs in the north must inevitably be greater than costs in the more populated southern areas. This, of course, does not excuse or justify lavishness, waste, or inefficiency, and since I have taken over the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources I have taken steps to ensure that

Supply-Northern Affairs the standards and scale of northern administration do not exceed those that are absolutely necessary, and that full advantage is taken of new techniques and new materials to achieve every possible economy, both in construction and operation. To do this, of course, involved securing the best available engineering advice. During the past two years, therefore, I have strengthened the engineering division of the department by securing a new chief of the division whose qualifications and northern experience are well known to some members of this house.
In the north one of the greatest factors in construction is the high cost of freight to the site. In order to minimize this, the bulk of our smaller buildings is now designed for prefabricated construction. This type of construction will reflect a considerable saving in freight costs, and in addition will greatly reduce erection costs. For the average size 2-bedroom house it is estimated that the initial construction will be 10 per cent lower than by normal construction methods. By using an advanced lightweight aluminum-clad prefabricated panel, maintenance and operation costs are being greatly reduced. Wherever possible buildings will be grouped to permit central heating, plumbing, and electrical services for further savings. In all-savings in construction, maintenance and fuel-there should be a reduction of at least 25 per cent, and I hope as high as 33 per cent. We are hopeful that this percentage reduction will be even greater in the more remote locations.
Due to severe climatic conditions the cost of heating our buildings is a major factor. Our new prefabricated designs specify materials with a high insulation value and an airtight seal between all panels. Further studies are being made of new materials and construction methods in order to achieve even greater economies and maximum space-to-weight ratio.
Bulk oil storage facilities are being introduced to a number of smaller settlements. In addition to reducing the cost of freight, the losses inherent in the use of fuel drums are eliminated. This alone should cut fuel costs at communities where bulk delivery is possible by at least 33 per cent. In the utilities field, the branch has arranged with Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to carry out studies of small atomic reactors capable of providing economical heat and light. The method of calling for construction tenders has been reviewed and significantly improved. At remote locations we have worked toward the objective of having the design and supply of materials one year, and construction the following year in order to take full advantage of climatic conditions.


We are working toward the earliest possible dates for tender calls. This will afford a greater opportunity for the interested contractors to visit the sites, to submit more realistic bids, and to get on the job early in the short construction season. New tendering procedures worked out by the Department of Public Works have greatly increased the number of contractors who are interested or actively engaged in northern construction.
I can assure the committee, Mr. Chairman, that my officials are more cost conscious than they have ever been. In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I am also fully conscious of my responsibilities in this regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister dealt very lightly with the estimates which we are considering at the present time, namely those of his own Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. However, he covered a wide field, all the way from wheat in the Department of Agriculture to the Department of External Affairs. In his usual manner he spoke vaguely and in general terms of the vision. Of course Mr. Chairman, I should say that his statement is certainly in keeping with the very little he has done about implementing this vision. Of course, there are reasons for this. The Oxford dictionary says that a visionary is a person able or accustomed to seeing visions; capable of receiving impressions by means of vision; given to fanciful and impractical views; speculative; dreamy, of schemes, plans, incapable of being carried out or realized; fantastic-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Were you referring to Mr. King there?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am speaking of you, sir. The definition continues: impractical; characterized by fancy or imagination without corresponding reality. This definition suits the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to a "T". I am sure the people of Canada will remember the many promises made during the last election campaign with regard to opening up the north. Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to spend too much time on these promises. However, I should like to outline briefly what this program meant in terms of roads and cost of those roads and to show the committee just how impractical this sort of policy is at this particular time.
Thousands of miles of road were promised. The total figure that I estimate it would cost this government to implement the roads they promised in the Northwest Territories is $200 million. The minister earlier said that the amount was $100 million. But his estimate now is as absurd as was the estimate he gave last year before the committee on mines, forests and waters of constructing a road from Flat Creek in the Yukon to some

place along the Arctic. At that time he told the committee that the cost of that road- with a good surface, at least according to him-would cost in the vicinity of $5 million to $8 million. This year, before the same committee discussing his estimates, the estimate is now doubled. I told the minister a year ago and I tell him today that the $100 million he suggests would not build all the roads that he promised during the election campaign. It will come closer to $200 million.
In any event, hon. members will recall that when the minister was before the committee on mines, forests and waters a year ago he told us that he had extended the roads program of the former administration by many more miles of roads than was suggested by the former administration to the Gordon commission in 1955.	He said that the only
difference between his government's program and that of the former government-in addition to that extra mileage of road-was that he intented to speed up and accelerate the road building. I should like to quote from page 16 of the evidence of that committee of Thursday, June 5, 1958. This is what the minister said in this regard at that time:
About the only thing that I did as minister was to bring these programs for 25 years down into a five-year program, that is as far as they affected the territories.
In other words he was going to speed up the former administration's program which included many miles of road and which I would say would have cost $100 million to $150 million. He is going to do this in five years.
In order to give the committee an idea of the areas those roads would serve, I will just refer to one particular proposal made by the minister, that of the road from Fort Reliance on the east arm of Great Slave lake to Eskimo Point on the west shore of Hudson bay. A road connecting these two points would be somewhere between 500 miles and 600 miles in length through rough, uninhabited and costly road building country. At the present time there are six persons living at Fort Reliance, four employed by the government and two trappers. At the other end of this road at Eskimo Point there are approximately 100 Eskimos and in the area in between a handful of people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Any igloos?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That could be. The area between these two communities has had little if anything done in the way of geological surveys. Hence we know little of its mineral potential. In speaking of this road to the northern Saskatchewan development conference in Saskatoon in November, 1957 the
Supply-Northern Affairs Saskatchewan Star-Phoenix, in reporting the minister's speech said this. This is referring to this particular road I have just mentioned. This is apparently an argument he advanced to justify the building of this road. This is what the newspaper says:
Though Mr. Hamilton would not name the area, he said that northwest of Eskimo Point there were fabulous from ore deposits, greater in extent than the Mesabi range that started and helped the United States to achieve its present great industrial development.
Mr. Chairman, the fabulous iron ore deposits of which the minister was apparently speaking were those at Rankin inlet where North Rankin Inlet Nickel Mines are now operating, and where, from what I know of the situation, they have been having their difficulties in extending their ore body to keep the mine producing at its present rate. The area in which that mine is operating was used by the minister, as I said before, to justify the building of this road.
Last fall, in a television program that I myself saw, a Mr. Webber, an official of North Rankin Inlet Nickel Mines appeared with the minister and a Dr. Byrd of McGill University and discussed this development program. During that television discussion Mr. Webber pointed out to the minister that a road program would not assist his company at Rankin inlet because of the fact that they are using, and will continue to use, the sea lanes which provide the cheapest means of transportation. But not too long after this program was carried by the C.B.C. the minister, speaking, in Saskatoon in September of 1958, apparently changed his tune. I should like to quote now from an article appearing in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of September 23, 1958 and headed "Mr. Hamilton's Northern Vision". A portion of this report reads as follows:
Mr. Hamilton described the U.S. atomic submarines Nautilus and Skate, as a new breed of ship which "in our lifetime", may revolutionize intercontinental maritime transport to an extent almost comparable to the changes brought about on land and in the air by the automobile and the aeroplane. He visualized submarine cargo ships coursing the world's oceans within 10 or 20 years and said Britain-
And this is the part I want the committee to take into consideration.
-already had submarine tankers and ore carriers on engineering drawing boards, the latter planned as carriers of Hudson bay iron.
That is the same iron ore that we are speaking of at Rankin inlet, the Hudson bay-ore.

When I was referring to the iron of the Hudson bay area, the reserves are very large. Everyone knows that the Rankin inlet mine is a zinc and copper mine, and nickel as well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Low grade iron. I think if the hon. members of the committee took a look at a map of the area it would be clear to them that the building of a road such as the one I have mentioned within the next few years certainly is visionary, and any person with such an idea could be considered impractical, fantastic and utterly devoid of corresponding realities. It also points out that the reference to the igloo to igloo road program of the government, made by my leader during the last election campaign, and which was related solely to the employment aspects of road building, may not be as far-fetched as a lot of people would like us to believe, even in other respects.
Let us now consider what has been done since this government took office, and what will be done this year according to the estimates now before us. First of all let us deal with what has been done and will be done this year in the Northwest Territories. The major project is the extension of the Mackenzie highway to Yellowknife. This road was started in 1956-57 by the former administration, and when this government took office approximately 90 miles had been built. The plan of the former administration was to complete this road by 1960, and I must say that the present government plans to do this according to the estimated figure for this year. In addition to this project they have carried on with the program of providing short access roads in the Wood Buffalo park to assist not only in their own work in the park but also for the benefit of the lumber and forest products industry in the same area. A road planned by the department some years ago between Fort Fitzgerald and Bell Rock, a distance of 28 miles, will also be built this year. In the Northwest Territories we find that for the first two years this government has been in office they will complete roads which were started by the former administration but not one single mile of the minister's so-called new road program has been started.
In fairness I must say that of benefit to the Northwest Territories the federal government and provincial government are now sharing on a 50-50 basis the rebuilding of certain stretches of the Mackenzie highway

within the province of Alberta, and for this I am sure the people of the Northwest Territories are very happy. In any event, the total to be spent this year in the Mackenzie district on roads will amount to $6,895,600. In addition to this I presume $1,500,000 will be the federal share of the rebuilding of the Mackenzie highway, making a total for all roads of $8,395,600.
In the Yukon last year, and planned for this year, bridges are being built on the highway between Whitehorse and Dawson city to give that area all year round transportation. The government has also carried on the plan of the former administration to improve the road from Johnsons Crossing to Ross river.
In addition to these are improvements on other minor access roads such as was done in the Northwest Territories in the Wood Buffalo park. Also included in this year's estimates is an amount to start construction of the only new road, and I am calling it a new road although it was included in the brief submitted to the Gordon economic commission by the former administration; but it is a new road in so far as this government will start its construction this year. This proposed road from Flat Creek in the Yukon, according to the answers received from the minister a year ago, in its first stages would run to Fort McPherson in the Northwest Territories, and from there eventually to the Arctic by way of Inuvik and the reindeer station.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I would like an assurance from the hon. member that he is not reading his speech.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am reading from very extensive notes, as did the minister, and I do not want to get off on a tangent and be called visionary. I want to be constructive today and to put up what I think is a good proposal to the minister.
During the past year since the preliminary surveys have been carried on we find the minister hedging and suggesting that the road may never get into the Fort McPherson area, at least according to the evidence he gave to the standing committee which dealt with these estimates a few weeks ago. According to the minister this road will do a great deal to open up the Peel plateau and Eagle plain areas for oil exploration and development purposes.
I would like to point out to the committee that exploration has been going on in this area since 1952 or thereabouts, and the companies operating in the area have previously built their own winter road over which

they have carried the bulk of their exploration equipment by tractor train. I am quite confident that any freight required by the oil companies in this area can in the future, as in the past, be taken over a winter road and any moneys spent should be spent to improve the present winter road so that trucks can do the transporting rather than tractor trains, and to build other winter roads that may be necessary. Some of these could originate from points along the Mackenzie river into areas that are considered potential oil producing areas.
To support this point of view I should like to quote from a speech given by Mr. Franc R. Jobouin, global consultant engineer with the Rio Tinto Company, and president of Bralorne Mines Limited to the northern development conference held in Edmonton last fall. Here is what Mr. Jobouin says in this regard:
All access and communication facilities should be improved. This calls as much for planning and co-ordination as it does for the spending of dollars. For example, why is our north, and particularly the geologically favourable areas, not laced with a network of "winter roads"? To the uninformed this simply means a 20-foot wide route, cut through the bush. Untrained labourers with axes and saws can do the job under supervision. No other improvement of the route is required, yet for the several winter months of each year that route can become an excellent highway over which tractor sled trains can haul freight as effectively as a railroad.
Of course a winter road such as Mr. Jobouin suggests would not be suitable for truck transport, but for very little money improvements could be made on such a road to allow for this type of transportation. If the area is finally found to be oil producing, and when the companies are in a position to market their oil, further improvements could be made to assist them in getting their development equipment into the area. Surely the minister does not suggest that when this time arrives the oil will be carried over this road in tank trucks rather than the modern method of pipe lines.
The total amount to be spent this coming year on roads and bridges in the Yukon will amount to $4,129,300. In addition to this there is the amount of $1,500,000 as the federal government's portion of the cost of the road from Stewart, British Columbia, to Cassiar. So, in both the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, including the federal share of the roads to resources program, a total of approximately $14 million will be spent. The greater portion of this amount will be spent to service and provide year round transportation to people in the already settled areas and in areas that are already producing and contributing to the national wealth of
Supply-Northern Affairs Canada; roads, I repeat, that with the exception of the Flat Creek to Peel plateau road, were started by the former administration.
I now return for a moment to the promises made during the 1958 election campaign. Thousands of miles of roads were promised for both the Yukon and Northwest Territories. According to the minister a large part of this program would be completed in five years. Two years will have passed and nothing particularly new will have happened.
The estimate for the Flat Creek to Peel plateau road is approximately $40,000 per mile, and some stretches of the road between Yellowknife and Hay River will run as high as $62,000 per mile. On the basis of this information I have estimated the cost of roads promised by this government at $200 million which is considerably in excess of what the minister stated. I simply give this information for the benefit of the committee. I suggest that this is a fair chunk of money and an amount that cannot be spent properly by this government without some advance planning as to where the roads should go.
The Canadian taxpayer including the taxpayer in northern Canada has the right to expect from this government that when roads are being built they will be built in areas that will assist industry to go into production for the benefit of the whole of the Canadian economy. Over a year ago I pointed out to the minister that before he went ahead spending the taxpayer's dollar on building roads, except in the already settled and producing areas, he should first find out by magnetic, electromagnetic and other scientific surveys the location of potential mineral wealth. This information should be published as soon as possible. Information of this kind should be made available to people who are interested in prospecting or in investing money in this field of resource development. This information should be given to people who, I am sure, if it can be pointed out to them that possibilities of oil and mineral deposits exist in a particular area will move into that area and do the necessary ground surveying, prospecting and drilling to determine whether or not the ore body is of commercial value.
Since I mentioned this a year ago the government have had representations from different organizations asking for an increase and an acceleration of the work done by the geological surveys branch of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. One of these representations was from the Royal Society of Canada and the Geological Association of Canada in the form of a brief submitted to cabinet urging an acceleration in this type of work. I might also quote again from the

Supply-Northern Affairs speech of Mr. Jobouin to the northern development conference in Edmonton last year in which he stated:
The excellent northern mapping work of the surveys branch and geological survey of Canada should be further accelerated, despite the marked improvement in recent years. Their results provide the very foundation on which all other development hinges.
I feel that airborne magnetic, electromagnetic, radiometric, and possibly the new airborne gravimetric surveying, on a reconnaissance scale, is a quite proper field for the federal and provincial governments to enter.
And again, just recently the report of the committee dealing with the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys recommended to the government an acceleration in this field. An immediate start on this type of survey could begin with areas adjacent to Mayo and Keno in the Yukon, and in the area between Yellowknife and the east arm of Grea-t Slave lake and the area northeast of Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories. I will not attempt to point out all the areas where this type of work should be carried on but in general the whole of the Northwest Territories and Yukon should be covered and the work done should be in areas of volcanic and sedimentary structure, ignoring the granite or so-called tombstone areas that have little or no possibilities. The results of such surveys would make it possible for the government or for anyone else, for that matter, to then outline a practical plan for development.
The second step, as I suggested a year ago, is to provide flight strips in the areas where prospectors or companies who wish to invest capital for exploration indicate they wish to explore. These people will then do the ground surveys and the necessary drilling that will indicate the size and value of the ore bodies.
The third step is to provide an incentive for the development companies to open up and bring the mines into production.
These incentives, I suggest, should be by way of increased income tax exemptions during the early years of the mines development. In this regard I wish to quote from a report in the Edmonton Journal reporting on a speech made by Mr. J. M. Botsford, general manager of Gunnar Mines Limited, to the northern development conference, and I quote:
Revised federal and provincial taxation rates, graduated according to latitude, would provide one of the greatest incentives for private enterprise to enter into this national project of developing the north and establishing northern communities," Mr. Botsford declared.
In addition to what Mr. Botsford said the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, and others, have submitted proposals
[Mr. Hardie.i

to the government to extend the present three-year tax free period in the case of new mines to five years for those mines operating above the 60th parallel.
I would also suggest to encourage prospecting of potential areas that prospectors be given some assistance to cover their transportation costs. An amount of $100,000 per year set aside in the estimates for this kind of assistance would encourage a great deal more prospecting and would be of great assistance to those people who have pioneered every major mineral discovery up to the present time.
Another point I might mention here that would be of assistance would be a relaxation in the regulations of the Department of Transport to speed up procedures for licensing of radio transmission stations for all mining exploration and development jobs.
In areas where there is potential the government should set out to survey the power potential, and the requirements for new mines. Also-and this matter I brought to the attention of the department some years ago-there should be an immediate review of the mining regulations in the Northwest Territories.
It seems that the practice has been that when a difficulty arises between an individual or company and the government in regard to the regulations the government passes an order in council to cover the particular situation without passing along the same advantages to everyone in the north by amending the regulations. These suggestions if implemented, will encourage capital to come into the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, will give the government a start on its inventory of resources, and will encourage the general development of the Northwest Territories and Yukon for the ultimate good of the whole of the Canadian nation.
The people presently living in the Northwest Territories, the pioneers of that vast country, also require some encouragement, and this I suggest can be done in a number of ways. For instance, along the Mackenzie and Liard rivers and in some of the communities around Great Slave lake, a large portion of the people are still attempting to derive their living from the fur industry. I do not think that members of this committee have to be told that these people cannot live on prices they receive for fur today. I would therefore suggest, as I have done on numerous other occasions, that the government make a serious study of what can be done about putting a floor price on fur, and in particular on muskrats, beaver and white fox. I see no reason why something along this line should not be done, in view

of the fact that so many products today are similarly covered under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
I submit it is only fair that the natives and trappers of the north should be given the same treatment. I do not know whether members of the committee realize the difficulties the people in those communities have in their day to day living. For instance, in the large majority of communities, the women, in order to do their washing and cooking, and so forth, are required to carry their water from the river up steep banks for great distances. To members of the committee this may seem to be a very minor detail, but it would certainly assist the large number of people in the country if pumping stations could be erected so that water could be pumped from the source of supply, the rivers or lakes, to the centres of those communities.
In many communities the people are isolated from the rest of the world at break-up and at freeze-up periods during the year. Transportation between those settlements is by float-equipped aircraft or by boat and canoe during the summer and by ski-equipped aircraft and dog team during the winter. During those periods of freeze-up and break-up, as in any community, emergencies can happen and many have happened over the years. For instance, what happens in a community at this time of the year when a person may have a ruptured appendix, a broken leg or some other sickness or accident and the closest doctor is possibly 200 or 300 miles away? The community may not have a nurse, but if there was one available what could she do in a serious case? I suggest that to remedy this sort of situation suitable air strips for the landing of aircraft such as the Cessna 180, the Beaver or Otter type be built at communities such as Fort McPherson, Fort Good Hope, Fort Norman, Fort Franklin, South Nahanni, Fort Liard, Jean Marie river, Rocher river, Snowdrift and Coppermine. These strips, I submit, would not be costly. They would run somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30,000 to $60,000 each, depending on the availability of a suitable site; in other words, for the same amount as, if not much more-

More frequent air service should also be given to places such as Fort Liard, South Nahanni, Fort Franklin, Rocher river and Snowdrift. The government could also build small floating wharves in each of these communities to assist in making it easier and safer for pontoon-equipped aircraft to dock during rough weather in the summer months. The government could also provide gas caches in communities where these services are not provided by the oil and gas dealers.
In the more settled areas such as Fort Smith, Hay River and Yellowknife, something should be done to give the industry and the people located there telephone communication with the outside world, something similar to the microwave plan that would also provide television for the area.
The government should also give serious consideration to the recommendation of the committee on mines, forests and waters suggesting amendments to the National Housing Act which would provide people living in northern Canada with a greater opportunity to enjoy the benefits of this act than is now the case.
While work on the suggestions I have outlined for surveys and other improvements is going on, the government could go forward with a roads program which would serve the present settled and producing areas of the north. In this regard I suggest that in the Northwest Territories the rebuilding of the Mackenzie highway should include hard surfacing the road from Grimshaw to Yellowknife. The proposed road connecting the Mackenzie highway with Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories should be proceeded with immediately, and any agreement with the provincial government of Alberta on this road should also include a program of hard surfacing. This road will serve not only the mixed farming area around Fort Vermilion, Alberta, but will also open up new forest areas and help considerably the sawmills and forest products industry operating in the Wood Buffalo park.
Construction should be undertaken of a winter road from the Mackenzie highway to the Fort Simpson area where a number of oil companies are operating at the present time and have been for the past five years engaged in extensive exploration programs. In other words, do for them what is being

Supply-Northern Affairs done for the companies operating in the Peel plateau and Eagle plain areas. Do something about the crossing of the Mackenzie highway at Hay River. Continue the road program as needed in the Wood Buffalo park and in the other communities in the territories. Bridge the Mackenzie river to make the road into Yellowknife an all year round proposition.
In the Yukon I suggest first that we should rebuild and hard-surface the road from Whitehorse to Keno; continue the program of co-operation with the province of British Columbia on the Stewart-Cassiar road; continue the present improvement to secondary roads such as the one from Johnsons Crossing to Ross river; make the road from Flat creek to Peel plateau and Eagle plain a winter road suitable for trucks, which would cut to present costs of $40,000 per mile to something around $20,000 per mile, and at the same time provide an adequate road for the people there who want to use it.
I might add that hard surfacing of the roads into Yellowknife, Fort Smith and Keno will give not only a better service to those areas but will result, I am sure, in reductions in truck freight rates, and a very considerable increase in the tourist industry. The high cost of living for people in these areas, and the high production costs of the various industries, will necessarily be reduced.
Mr. Chairman, after outlining the things that should be done, it would be natural to expect that members of this committee would ask, how is this proposal to be financed and that information I intend to give the committee now. The program I have outlined could be based on a six-year period. The program could be started next year and completed before March 31, 1966. First of all, I will give the estimated costs for the roads program in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. The amounts estimated for the Northwest Territories are as follows. I wonder whether it would be possible for this statement to be put in Hansard in tabular form so that it would be easier for persons to read? I have a table here which I could place in Hansard if the committee will permit it.

That is a total for major roads in both territories of $68 million. Then I come to the other projects I have suggested.
1.	Estimated cost of other community and park roads, $2,600,000.
2.	Wharves and pumps, $100,000.

That is the cash part of my proposal. That is what it would cost the national treasury in six years. The other proposals, such as amendments to the National Housing Act, mining regulations and radio regulations, cost nothing. Nothing is taken from the national treasury by extending the present three-year tax free period for new mines to five years. If the mines are not opened, the treasury gets nothing. The gas caches as proposed would be handled on the same basis as an oil dealer would handle them, costing nothing to the national treasury.
To sum up, over a period of six years a total of $84 million would be spent, or $14 million per year. This amount of $14 million is equal, if members of the committee will recall, to the total to be spent on roads in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon this year. The figure I have given of $14 million a year will not increase the estimates for this branch one nickel to carry out the suggestions I have made, and with no increase in the annual expenditures of the department we can help the people living in the country at the present time to enjoy some of the amenities enjoyed by people in the rest of Canada which I am sure they justly deserve. Complete a six-year program of surveying and mapping and that should give the department some idea of where future roads should

go. I propose that $6 million be spent on this over and above what the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is now spending.
This program, as I said before, will accelerate the inventory of our resources. It will encourage investment capital to come into the area. It will help prospectors and bring the roads that are built in this period up to a standard that will encourage freight rate reductions and further encourage investment in the area. It will help to give a real boost to the tourist industry, which I know is close to the minister's heart.
And do not forget this. It will leave the government with $116 million of the $200 million it would have required to fulfil its election promises for the rebuilding of roads and air strips as they are needed. I ask members of the house if this is not a sound policy. Would not the government be better off to announce a policy such as this and admit the mistakes they made in their promises of 1958 rather than try to cover up these phony visions by putting up smokescreens such as the minister has in the past few months by his attempts to take the eyes of the Canadian people away from that great area of our northern mainland, that area where the vision was born, lying between the northern boundaries of the four western provinces and the Arctic?
Why, I ask, put up smokescreens to direct the attention of the people of Canada to the Arctic islands and to a so-called oil boom which, in fact, is just a real estate play where a large number of the individuals and companies have been given millions of acres in the Arctic islands without putting up a plugged nickel? Nor have any large number of these individuals and companies shown the government that they have the financial wherewithal to do any amount of exploration work as required by the regulations. Why the excitement in this area when we cannot get rid of the oil we are producing in Alberta at the present time?
The minister's stories of submarines carrying oil and iron ore that we have not explored as yet under the polar ice cap are visions that may be accomplished some time in the distant future. If he wants to get excited about something let him get excited about doing something now. Do something in the immediate future rather than getting steamed up over what may happen 40 or 50 years from now. While I am on the subject of visions and the Arctic islands, I should like to make a suggestion to the minister. He should not let these visions run away with him or he may find that his next vision will put him right in the middle of Siberia. I would not want to wish him anything like 66968-9-368
Supply-Northern Affairs that but if he goes any farther north with the vision that is where he will be. The $50 million skyscraper city at Frobisher bay, where the minister says the people will be employed refuelling aircraft and the Eskimos will be busy selling their carvings to European and American tourists while the planes are being refuelled, comes far short of being a practical idea. That is particularly so when we consider that long-range jet aircraft are now being flown non-stop from London to New York and in a very short space of time we can expect they will be flying non-stop from London and Amsterdam to Edmonton and Winnipeg. I submit that by the time this townsite is built this could happen and the $50 million spent might just as well have been thrown into the middle of Great Slave lake. I am confident that the $50 million could be spent on other practical northern projects or to help the economy of the Atlantic provinces or other parts of Canada.
The government continues to deal with the roads program by now focusing attention on the Arctic islands and deals with the promise made not only in the election but also in the speech from the throne a year ago concerning the building of the railroad to Pine Point by setting up a commission. If the minister really wants to settle this problem of a railroad to the satisfaction of everyone concerned I would suggest to him that the government start immediately to build the railway from Grimshaw to Fort Vermilion and then to Fort Smith, which would tap the agricultural lands between Grimshaw and Vermilion and open up a large area for lumber and forest products. Then, if and when the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company want to open up their mine at Pine Point, extend the railway to Pine Point either from Fort Smith or from Fort Vermilion. The railway would serve the immediate needs of the agricultural and forest industries and would cost approximately the same amount as a railway from Waterways or Grimshaw to Pine Point.
The cost of the additional rail, if and when the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company want to open their mine, would be between $12 million and $16 million, based on the figures given by the minister at various times on the cost per mile of rail in that part of the country. It is reasonable to believe that if we delay the building of this railroad the cost will be a great deal higher than the estimated cost today. My point, therefore, Mr. Chairman, is that if the railroad were started immediately, rather than 10, 15 or 20 years from now, the extra mileage costs suggested in the route I have now proposed would be saved.

I hope the minister will give serious consideration to these suggestions. I do not intend to take any more time at this stage, but will make further comments when we proceed to discussion of the various items before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, we have a phrase to the effect that without vision the people perish. Now, we have a double vision and I am sure it is going to be a "Hardie" one and that both aspects of the duplicity are going to be around for a long time. I must compliment the hon. member upon preparing such a serious and weighty speech. I have been wondering where he has been lately, since he has been missing from our meetings of the mines, forests and waters committee. Now I know he was getting ready for this great effort. I must say that the tone of the address was most surprising and very pleasing.
The hon. member concentrated on northern administration. I must confess that when the report of our committee came into the house I was bitterly disappointed at the way it was picked up and carried across the country. I believe most of the people in the committee, certainly most of the people from British Columbia and Ontario anyway, thought that by far the most important recommendation of that committee had to do with forestry and the forestry branch, and that there was a disproportionate amount of attention given to the other aspects of the committee report. I certainly hope that the minister, at least, will recognize that this was the order of importance in the minds of the committee, and will take his closest and hardest look at those recommendations dealing with forestry and not with northern administration.
I did not have any opportunity to take part in preparing that section of the report, but I would not deny that as a member of the committee I went along with the rest of them in unanimously adopting the report.

speechtext:
The hon. member did not vote for the report, and that is fine, but I would have gone along with it, I believe. I am much perturbed about the effect one particular section of this report may have. I think it may leave members of parliament open to criticism for perhaps shooting before they can see their target. I have reference to the fact that a subcommittee was supposed to make a visit into the north in order to see the installations, since we had no outside witnesses, that is outside the government administration on this particular phase, in contrast

to the large number of witnesses we had on other aspects of departmental activities. I think we would have been in a much more solid position if we had actually seen the area.
Now, this question of a subcommittee of the House of Commons going to visit regions that are important to a department is something to which we have to give immediate, serious consideration. It is all very well for us to sit down in a smoky room and examine or cross-examine people from the department. However, I believe unless we can get out onto the ground and see many of the problems, the institutions, the type of construction that is being done, the type of people who are involved in it, we are really not in a prime position to make any lucid or intelligent comments or recommendations. I hope, for that reason, the minister will give urgent consideration to seeing that a subcommittee of this committee is given the power, under the Inquiries Act, to visit the area this fall before the weather closes in, and have a look at those installations which the committee did, to a degree, criticize, and have a look at this administration that, to a degree, the committee has criticized.
I could welcome some kind of investigation or committee excursion to the various forest experiment places, and visits to competitive areas such as the lake states and the southern states. However, in that particular field at least some of the members of the committee have had experience and they do have intimate knowledge of the problems of the pulp and paper industry and the lumbering industry. In so far as the north is concerned, with the exception of the two hon. members of parliament who come from there we are-I was going to say an ignorant lot-an uninformed group relatively at the present time. I believe this is one of the best things the minister could do or that the government could do, and one of the best things I think that could happen for northern administration, would be to have a small subcommittee given the opportunity to go as soon as possible to these places and have an opportunity of examining witnesses, looking into things closely. I certainly hope the minister will express himself in this particular regard.
In so far as the vision is concerned, I think the vision helped to win an election. I do not know, but I believe it is going to lose the next election that is coming up in a few years. It has always been my feeling that this vision was oversold. I can give you an example of the reaction of the part of the country I represent, and the reason I say I think it was oversold. I am reading from an editorial in our local newspaper at Port Arthur, the

News-Chronicle, which includes a quotation from a gentleman who is the manager of the northwestern Ontario development association, and who has been called the William Jennings Bryan of the north. When you hear this quotation, I think you will see why. He says:
Parliament, awake! Open up central Canada with a railway and highway to connect your new fresh water seacoast of lake Superior and the salty bays of Hudson and James, tapping natural wealth for nearly 1,000 miles between them.
Build access roads into areas of favourable geological formations, conifer forests and power sites.
Extend the network of roadlinks to lakes, rivers and granite hills of spectacular scenic value to attract an ever increasing flow of vacationing travellers from south of the border into our unique hinterland.
Encourage and assist a new wave of settlement and venture capital to populate and develop the glittering potential of the region.
Under such a dynamic policy, this central section of the nation-populated and productive- will stand a generation hence a magnificent monument to the far-reaching vision of its chosen leaders and a reservoir of economic strength and security in the hazardous era stretching into the foreseeable future of the world.
This gentleman is talking about that vast region lying north of lake Superior, running 600 to 800 miles north to Hudson bay, and the fact it is not developed yet, is largely untapped. It has one advantage over the area about which the minister's department is excited and interested, it has fairly substantial coniferous forests. When you examine the reasons why our government should take an interest in the north, I think primarily one comes down to the question of defence and national sovereignty as interrelated things, and the sheer fact we are in competition with the Russians. I do not believe that the competition and defence end should blind us to the fact that our Arctic is different from the Russians' Arctic.
The next thing in which we need to be interested, I think, is looking after our native people. The third thing in which we are interested in so far as the north is concerned is the possibility of some economic return from the region. The only economic return one can see from the north is in the mineral resources. The great problem there, and the minister in effect admitted it before the committee hearings, is the cost factor.
In the north costs are very high, especially in connection with any kind of mineral and in the oil and gas field. In fact, the oil and gas field in the Arctic, as the hon. member for Mackenzie River pointed out, is highly speculative. It really does not apply in great substance. When you consider that we have in the southern part of Canada forest resources that are still unused and all sorts of mineral deposits that are unused to get 66968-9-368i
Supply-Northern Affairs overly excited and to project a vision, as this particular government did in order to win an election or associated with winning an election, you are carrying out in effect a bit of tomfoolery.
Look after the native people as well, make sure that our defence and our sovereignty are established. But to give the impression that the thing for the young men of Canada to do today is to go north and that going north means away north, I think you are doing a disservice to the country. The majority of people who I have encountered who have come back from the north say that with the exception of the odd mounted policeman and the odd Hudson Bay man these people who live up there look upon themselves as temporary visitors. I think the turnover in the various northern departments that have anything to do with the north indicate that this is so.
I know the minister, with his vision to the future and to planning, may insist that I am being pessimistic and destructive. That is fair enough. But I just feel that in this whole area the minister and his department may have become completely out of focus as to what should be a more prime responsibility. I think of that prime responsibility as being reflected in this report of the mines, forests and waters committee. I refer to the report on forestry. I certainly hope that there will not become a disbalance in his department of northern affairs through forgetting that there are immense responsibilities open to the forestry side. I think one of the steps the minister should take as soon as possible is to appoint an associate deputy minister for the forestry operations.
The forestry recommendations were supported by a fair volume of evidence. I just wanted to deal with one of the points or one of the recommendations suggesting that we need a forest taxation study. That is something I believe we have needed for a long time. With all due respect to the very resourceful and capable industrial people who appeared before the committee, my sympathies with them in their position or in their appeals for tax relief are not going to be consolidated until we have such a study because I do not know whether we can really believe them. I do not mean that they are lying but I think that they may be taking a sort of over gloomy position in the face of a competition to which they are not accustomed. I would not make this as a charge but I think this may be possible and it points up all the more reason why we should have this taxation study and in my opinion have it in a hurry. I certainly hope that the minister will see that it goes beyond something

Supply-Northern Affairs which is in his department and that is it is a responsibility of the Minister of Finance.
One of the aspects of the department upon which I should like to touch is a rather delicate one. It is a question of the national museum and the fact that an appointee of the previous administration or a man who was appointed by the previous administration has left at the minister's request. I think it is fair to say that that man, whatever his actions in the department, whatever may have been his competence and his duties, is now as a result of the minister's action under a great cloud in so far as his ability and his whole attitude toward work and administration are concerned. In other words I am suggesting to the minister he has in effect ruined the career of a man who ostensibly or apparently had achieved something in the scientific field. When one reads all the correspondence and all the answers to questions that have been given by the department in relation to this whole problem and they would fill pages of the order paper, and when one reads the statement of Mr. Rousseau involved in this matter it quickly becomes apparent that there are a number of sides to this question. I would not want to come in here and lay down the line and say that Dr. Rousseau has been completely vicitimized by anyone. However, the thing that bothers me -and I will say it to the minister-is that there seems to be something very tawdry in the whole set-up of the way this man was appointed.
I do not like the background and the information that is revealed with regard to the part played by one of the former officials, namely Mr. Lamontagne. I do not like the part that seems to have been played by Mr. Lesage, the former minister in getting this man into the department, getting him a job and leading him to believe that he had certain responsibilities and a certain future. Then we get this quick about-face; a remarkable about-face for a civil servant. I think the minister will agree that within a remarkably short period of time here was a man who was wooed into a job and then he was in trouble very quickly and within a relatively short time he got the boot.
It is a confused situation and I am certainly not ever going to be in a position to get to the roots of it, nor do I think are any other hon. members. I should just like to suggest to the minister that if his actions in this particular affair were based on complete justice or an attitude or wish to have complete justice for this particular man, the *events could have gone along in a different path. As the situation is now, I understand the gentleman is going to have great difficulty in getting any kind of employment. To my


way of thinking, if he is to be condemned, the departmental administration before the present minister's time is to be condemned. I almost have the hunch that somehow the minister in order to protect some of his civil servants, has been masking over what I think are mistakes made by the previous minister and the previous administration in this particular field.
I do not know where one can go along this particular line but I certainly think that the recommendations of the committee, in so far as the national museum is concerned should be taken up. I think it is a very sad situation when, whatever the capacities a man may have had, he is encouraged or asked to resign and it appears that one of the main factors in the resignation is that we have in the department some foreign nationals who disagreed with him. This may not be the whole story. Those foreign nationals may not have much responsibility for the matter. But the fact remains that they are foreign nationals or a couple of them were. To me this is a sad situation. That is one of the reasons why I should like to see the minister do something about the recommendation so that we can get to the stage where we have Canadian anthropologists and experts whom we can have running our museum instead of having this dependence on Americans.
The only reiteration I should like to make in my remarks, Mr. Chairman, is this. I should like the minister to consider seriously this question of a committee visit to the north. I should like him to express his opinion on the recommendations the committee made in connection with the northern mines administration. If the committee does not get an opportunity of visiting the north this session, I certainly hope he will do what he can to see that it gets that opportunity in the next session. In the next year I think we shall all be greatly interested in seeing what comes of what the minister has referred to as a frank report.
If the minister does follow up the recommendations, especially of the forests department, I think he will find an even more enthusiastic committee than he has had this year. I have been a member of five committees in this house and this committee has been the best of all of them in the sense of attendance and interest of the members, and their willingness to work on their own to bone up on things, I think has been exemplary. I would hope that the minister would give this kind of good, solid committee, with a chairman who to me has had a very open mind with a fair lack of the more serious kind of partisanship, a real boost for its

future by carrying out as many as possible of its recommendations in the coming months.
