Mr. Chairman, at this point I would like to take a few minutes of the committee's time to speak about the Canadian government travel bureau and tourist spending. I prefer to make my remarks at this stage rather than on the individual items because the remarks I will make are of general interest and refer to the responsibilities of the department generally concerning the tourist industry.
The minute we start talking about tourism, I realize that the Minister of Finance clutches at his purse strings and starts worrying about our request for loans to tourist operators. I am sorry that such an idea has got across to the Minister of Finance because there are many more problems in the tourist industry than tourist loans. That may be a means to an end, but I want to refer to the larger field. I think the tourist industry can bring this country out of the red financially if properly handled and can give us a big boost in our foreign dollar receipts. We can make the Minister of Finance happy, I believe, rather than sad if we carry out some of the ideas concerning tourism which have been put forward by the mines, forests and waters committee when they dealt with this particular subject. We can bring in firstly hundreds of millions of dollars, foreign money, which is new or found money, in addition to circulating more quickly Canadian funds by people travelling within Canada. So I want to talk about money matters in connection with the tourist industry rather than dealing in detail with what has been discussed before.
The tourist industry is the third largest producer of foreign dollars in Canada. At the top of the list is newsprint, and for 1957, which was the latest poll, the figure for a comparative basis for newsprint was $715 million, which was foreign money. The second was wheat, which brought in $380 million, and the third was travel, which produced $363 million. Below those three items came pulp, lumber, aluminum, iron ore, petroleum and uranium. Each of those latter mentioned articles bring in less foreign dollars than does the tourist industry. One source of concern is that our travel income declined in 1958 to $352 million, which is down $11 million, or approximately 3 per cent.
In this connection I would like to make some comparisons. I know that comparisons are odious in a lot of cases, but I think we must consider this matter in the light of financial return. I would like to compare for a moment the subject of wheat, which brings
Private Bills
in approximately the same number of foreign dollars, a little more, than travel. I would like to ask the committee how many millions of dollars we lay out on wheat each year. For prairie farm assistance, $500,000; under the farmers' rehabilitation act, $5 million. Then there is the new crop insurance, farm loans, a large portion of the expenditures of the Department of Agriculture amounting to $106 million, and a large chunk of the expenditures of the Department of Trade and Commerce at $64 million. I am not going to total those figures up because the figure would rather astound us, but the return is about the same as for the tourist industry. And we spend for the tourist industry just a little more than $2 million to bring back an almost equivalent return as wheat.
I do not want to dwell on wheat because it is only one of a number, but I am appalled at the large number of non-productive spending items which we find in our estimates; money for which we have no return, money which is merely spread around, received from one source and put to another. The tourist industry is a producer of money. The government is not in business to make money. On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, I submit that we are not in business to lose money any faster than necessary, either.
I see that it is nearly five o'clock and I want to go on to another portion of my address at this point. However, I just want to remind the committee that tourist spending has declined and also tourist income has declined, and I think it is most essential that we bear the comparisons I have just made in mind when we consider estimates in the future. May I call it five o'clock.
Progress reported.

The house in committee on Bill No. S-29, to incorporate Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company-Mr. Dorion-Mr. Rea in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could put a question to the sponsor of this bill and ask him if he could explain to the

Private Bills
committee what jurisdiction he thinks this parliament has in the field of insurance?

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to answer the hon. gentleman's question. I know that this question of insurance has been discussed for a long time and there have been some judgments by the privy council the last of which I believe was in 1932 and was to the effect that it is within the jurisdiction of the provinces to occupy the field of insurance, but after that the federal law was changed. If you look at the statutes you can see that there is no obligation for an insurance company to be constituted in virtue of the federal law.
I do not know about the other provinces but in Alberta it is absolutely necessary for an insurance company to have a federal licence to carry on business in that province. That is the only purpose of this bill.
No doubt the hon. gentleman is familiar with that patriotic movement Caisse Popu-laire Desjardins which has many clients and customers in Alberta. They cannot operate with their provincial company because that province requires a federal licence. That is the only purpose of this bill. I do not believe we can deprive that important organization of the right to carry on business in Alberta or in the other provinces.
Is the hon. member quite satisfied that parliament in enacting this measure-if indeed parliament does enact it as I suppose it will-is not in any way infringing upon provincial autonomy?

I would not like to argue that point. If the hon. member refers to the last judgment of the privy council, which was the case of the Citizens' Insurance Company, I believe he will find that the wording leaves the question open. The sense of that judgment is only that the federal authorities cannot oblige any provincial insurance company to operate without a federal licence. I believe that is the general meaning of that judgment, but I would not like to assure the hon. member that the privy council by that judgment has completely shut the door to federal jurisdiction.
But the hon. gentleman is satisfied, then, that we are not doing anything that is in any way an attack upon provincial autonomy?
I am satisfied that from a practical point of view it is absolutely necessary to have a federal statute.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. McGee for the second reading of Bill No. C-19, to amend the Criminal Code (corporal punishment). (Translation):

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity of making a few remarks about the act to amend the Criminal Code (corporal punishment).
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record of the house one of the explanatory notes which reads as follows:
The Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on capital punishment, corporal punishment and lotteries, which reported in June and July 1956, recommended, inter alia, that corporal punishment be abolished for any of the offences for which it is presently described in the Criminal Code.
Mr. Speaker, we have to realize that this bill proposes to amend only sections 136, 138, 141, 142, 148, 218, 289, 292, 586 and 641 of the Criminal Code.
Mr. Speaker, I would like all the hon. members to understand that when we discuss a matter such as corporal punishment, the government must have the co-operation of everyone, in the circumstances.
(Text):
In discussing this legislation before the house this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say first of all that very generally I tend to think of corporal punishment under three different headings. We see, first of all, where a person could be sentenced for various crimes under the Criminal Code and the sentence could include corporal punishment. This should be distinguished from the corporal punishment that can be administered under the Penitentiary Act, for example. Also, in a more general way, we can consider

that aspect of corporal punishment which can be administered, for example, to a young offender without actually sending him to prison.
The first thing that I should like to touch upon at the present time is something that has been notably impressed upon me. I have read the House of Commons and Senate committee report which was brought out in 1956, and many comparisons have been made by statistics with conditions in the United Kingdom. We all know that in 1948 the United Kingdom abolished corporal punishment, but I feel it is perhaps false for us to make statistical comparisons in the field of penology, notably with the United Kingdom experience in corporal punishment. I regret to say it, but the United Kingdom has been able to make many sweeping reforms such as this one with regard to corporal punishment which we have not been able to make. Again, I regret to say that after 22 years of Liberal rule we were away behind in the field of prison reform.
It was stated in this house not so long ago-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: We have had two years of Conservative rule.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
It was stated in this house by many members not so long ago that when the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) took over his portfolio he found, both as regards the physical plant of our prisons and as regards many specific reforms, that we were lagging far behind as a nation.
While I seem to be straying very far into the general field of criminology and penology, I feel that corporal punishment must be discussed with this general background knowledge. Many people have mentioned to me -and I am sure to many other hon. members of this House of Commons-that the discussion of capital punishment, corporal punishment and prison reform in general is a timeworn and time-beaten subject; but still, that does not mean that much has been done; that also does not mean that much more does not remain to be done before we as Canadians can be at all satisfied with the state of criminal reform in general.
In discussing such subjects as corporal and capital punishment, I think too many of us tend to be on extreme sides of the subject. A lot of people feel that the public looks upon corporal punishment as retribution. I have a little more faith in human nature than that. I do not think that any hon. member of this House of Commons, or any citizen of Canada wants to see a man whipped. I know I do not and I am absolutely sure that everybody in this House of Commons shares the same opinion.
Criminal Code
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I believe in the collective theory of guilt. Whenever I see a man sentenced, no matter for what crime, I always feel that although man is a little lower than the angels but yet a little higher than the rest of the animal kingdom, we must realize that there is such a thing as individual responsibility in this day and age. At the same time, when I see a man sentenced to prison I do believe in the collective theory of guilt. While he is individually responsible I believe, ofttimes, general social and economic conditions brought about the state of affairs which have sent him along the road to crime. I know in my own case, in the little prison work that I have had the opportunity to do, I have often looked at some of the young men I have worked with and said to myself, "There but for the grace of God go I".
At the same time, I turn back to the point that I do not think we should over-emphasize the fact that the public at large, even though these things are given a lot of publicity and so forth, are at any time taking a retributive look at this problem.
In discussing corporal punishment at this time, I ask myself one basic question. Does corporal punishment act as a deterrent to other individuals in society? Does it help to cure the prisoner himself? In other words, does it help to abolish recidivism? In the light of these questions which I ask myself and in the light of the House of Commons and the Senate committee report which was brought down in 1956, I do feel that I should like very sincerely to support the legislation which has been brought before us today.
I should point out that in 1931 corporal punishment was meted out in only 12.1 per cent of the cases in which it might have been used under the Criminal Code. In 1954 it was used in only .6 per cent of the cases. If those in authority feel that this legislation should not be passed at the present time, I would like to emphasize right here and now that corporal punishment should be used only after a thorough background investigation of the man charged has been undertaken. I should like to point out, as the committee said, that if it is to be used at all, either under or outside of the terms of the Criminal Code, it should be applied early in the sentence. At the same time I think it should be made quite clear to the public that it is used only on very rare occasions under the present set-up. I think a lot of us have known of the picture of a man being struck down by a cat-o-nine-tails until he is knocked unconscious, and all that sort of thing.
Such is not the case. Today a medical examination is involved. The punishment is

Criminal Code
administered with a proper strap or certainly should be and it is done in the presence of a doctor.
Realizing that at the present time we are only discussing corporal punishment as it relates to the Criminal Code, I am very happy to support the legislation now before us. At the same time I should like to say that under the Penitentiary Act and similar legislation for provincial prisons there is undoubtedly a good argument for retaining corporal punishment for misbehaviour in the case of those confined to a prison, but it should be realized that is not what we are discussing this afternoon.
After many chats with various individuals, and I know that my remarks are not entirely in agreement with the report of the Senate and House of Commons committee in 1956, I think there is a good argument to be put forward today, because even since 1956 we have seen a tremendous increase in juvenile delinquency from one end of the country to the other. I am not too sure, for example, that it would not be helpful if magistrates were to hand out as a punishment a good birching in the case of many young people who do not seem to want to conform to normal social behavior. But at the same time, going back to the specific terms of the legislation before us, realizing that in later years much progress has been made in psychiatric development, realizing that the public also realizes that while a man is individually responsible we are not proving anything unless we cure him while he is in prison, I believe, having that point of view before me, that this legislation should be supported.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also am glad to add my voice to those who support this legislation. I fully realize that it was originally introduced in the house by a neighbour of mine, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), and I should like to quote from Hansard for June 6, 1958, page 935, when he made his opening statement on the bill. At that time he called attention to the fact that article 5 of the universal declaration of human rights adopted by the United Nations and supported by Canada reads as follows:
No one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
The hon. member went on to say:
In view of this provision in the universal declaration of human rights of the United Nations which has been accepted by Canada it is difficult to understand how Canadians could give formal approval to that provision and yet retain corporal punishment under our criminal law.
He pointed out that in the western world the only countries he knew of which retained
[Mr. Grafftey.l
corporal punishment as part of their criminal law were South Africa and Canada. For further information I went, as other members have done, to the proceeding of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which sat during 1954 and 1955. The total amount of evidence is over 1,600 pages, and although the evidence deals not only with corporal punishment but also with capital punishment and lotteries, by far the greater amount of the evidence had to do with capital and corporal punishment. I should like to read a few excerpts from some of the evidence given to the committee. I was interested in the submission of the United Church of Canada presented by the Rev. J. R. Mutchmor, secretary of the board of evangelism and social service. It is found on page 531 of the evidence taken in 1954. He said:
We believe it is both the right and duty of the United Church of Canada as a branch of the Christian church to co-operate with the state in a common effort to determine the best methods to deal with crime including those redemptive processes essential to the restoration of the criminal. We believe also in stressing the need for and value of preventive work and the importance of all character building methods and programs as the best way to reduce crime. We believe, in short, that only the good way of life can effectively overcome the evil ways. We would accentuate not the prohibitive and penalizing methods, some of which are necessary, but the positive and character building ones.
As found on page 533 he went on to say:
We regret that at the present level of progress in correctional work the use of corporal punishment as a last resort may be a necessity. We believe that the state should look forward to its abolition. If the state cannot see its way to do this at the present juncture in correctional work, it should continue its inquiries and research, making a project of the task of the gradual elimination of this form of punishment which is most degrading to human dignity, both for those who inflict it and those upon whom it is inflicted.
Warden Christie, warden of the Oakalla prison, British Columbia, who is an outstanding penologist and formerly a social worker, and who has made a tremendous contribution to penology in British Columbia, was a witness before the committee, and I believe that because of his background what he had to say should be of interest to the house. As found on page 573 he said with respect to corporal punishment:
There are better and less dangerous means of control, but it would be a mistake to take corporal punishment as a means of control away from an institution if it had no other means of control at its disposal.
In this case he was talking of corporal punishment as a means of control of inmates in an institution and he agreed that this was necessary in certain instances, as the previous

speaker has also indicated. He did say, however, that institutions which have rooms provided for complete segregation or disassociation such as are used in a mental institution have no need of corporal punishment. He pointed out that corporal punishment in penitentiaries and other corrective institutions was diminishing. However, with regard to corporal punishment as a form of punishment inflicted under the Criminal Code he was very forthright in his condemnation. He said as found on page 570:
X believe further that it will soon be impossible for a people who have our present scientific knowledge at their disposal to retain either corporal or capital punishment as methods of control. It will, however, in my estimation, take some time for our present knowledge to extend to the point where we realize how illogical, unnecessary and socially damaging it is to continue their use.
The point that Warden Christie made was that corporal punishment was ineffective, that it actually prevented the redemption of the criminal. It embittered him against society and made the corrective work of the institution that much harder to accomplish. I was interested also in a statement made by Mr. Kirkpatrick of the John Howard society of Ontario. This is found on page 596, where he pointed out that the severity of punishment as a deterrent is a fallacy. He went back into the history of Anglo-Saxon society to show that the very severe punishment given for relatively trivial offences had no result whatever in the reduction of crime. He said:
It is commonly said that punishment has three principle purposes-retribution, deterrence and reformation. Of these it is generally conceded that retribution should no longer assume a place in modern penology. But any system of penology must maintain, as its fundamental basis, the protection of society.
He pointed out in regard to the published statistics, in the same way as the previous speaker pointed out, that judges are very loath to add whipping to imprisonment sentences. He was speaking of the period 1949-1950-1951, when the total number of convictions for robbery in Canada was between 700 and 900 and the number of whippings ordered by the courts amounted to something less than one per cent of those cases. He said that the common objective of all concerned in this whole process should be the protection of society by the rehabilitation of the offender. He went on to state that whippings did not help in this regard but actually hindered this rehabilitation work.
Finally, I should like to point out the evidence as given by Major General R. B. Gibson before this committee in 1955. The evidence will be found on page 292. Major General Gibson was commissioner of penitentiaries, and he had this to say:
66968-9-369
Criminal Code
The infliction of corporal punishment is a most distasteful task for all who are responsible for it, both those who have the responsibility of deciding whether it should be authorized, and those who have the duty of carrying it out. Happily, in recent years its award by the courts and its use as a disciplinary measure in the penitentiaries has been decreasing.
Continuing his statement, he said:
My own view, and I am expressing only my personal feelings in the matter, is that corporal punishment should not be awarded as part of the sentence of the court. The court has the opportunity of awarding a sentence of more or less imprisonment when a person has been convicted, and in my view the fear of imprisonment for a lengthy period is a sufficient deterrent for those who contemplate the commission of a crime without adding to it the fear of corporal punishment-
I do not consider that an award of corporal punishment as part of the sentence is a really effective method of preventing the commission of criminal offences because when such an award is made as part of the sentence a considerable period of time must elapse before the penalty can be inflicted. There must be time for an appeal, and whether there is an appeal or not, the time allowed for such appeal must elapse before the punishment can be inflicted. There is therefore a considerable period before the penalty is carried out, and it cannot be directly related to the offence. Corporal punishment, to be effective as a deterrent, must follow closely after the commission of the offence for which it is inflicted.
Then, he goes on to state:
If in addition to the sentence of imprisonment which involves loss of liberty and separation from his family and home ties, corporal punishment as part of his sentence has to be inflicted by the persons who are seeking to help him to readjust himself and his thinking to prepare for his release, it is evident that it will be difficult to convince him that these efforts are sincere.
It is a rather strange fact that corporal punishment is still left in our code in the face of the evidence contained in these two volumes which represents the evidence given to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons. This idea of revenge is something that should be, and I believe is, foreign to most Canadians. Prison sentences are set up for punishment, and whipping is something extra that is added. As the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) has pointed out, in something less than 1 per cent of the cases where a judge could order a whipping, were such sentences given. This means that court officers themselves are unwilling to use the provision in the code. It is, therefore, a law which is not being applied because those who are empowered to apply it, in the great majority of instances, do not wish to apply it. They do have the right to either order a whipping or not order it.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this bill should receive general support from all quarters in this house. I suggest the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) should take note of

Criminal Code
the remarks that have been made in this debate and at as early a time as possible something should be done toward bringing our Criminal Code more in line with that of the nations with whom we feel we are on an equal plane.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time I have spoken in this house on corporal punishment. I have seen no reason for changing my attitude to this inhuman treatment of a fellow human being. If we go back to the early days of history, there may have been some justification for the use of force in trying to deter crime or in punishing criminals once they were caught. However, in a civilized society this is clearly out of date. We have to make up our minds, I think once and for all, just where justice is going. I think there is no longer a need for revenge in our system of justice. Revenge is negative, and although an individual who has been wronged, whether personally or through his loved ones or through his property, has a natural jungle instinct for revenge, most civilized men and certainly civilized society has no such aim.
As lawmakers surely we want to be practical. Anything which has no positive results is a waste of time. If we have statutes which are outmoded it is our clear duty to get rid of them. If our statutes need remodelling, we are the only people who have the opportunity or, indeed, the duty to do it. Perhaps people might wonder why a law enforcement officer should take such a peculiar attitude because the general attitude of policemen, I think, is not imaginative.
Policemen are often thought to be the strong arm of the law and punitive but I do not think this is any longer the case. Certainly I can speak for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in which body I served. Their general attitude is not one of punishment or revenge, but rather one of prevention. People will respect the mounted police and the other police forces only in so far as they are humane and fair. I suggest that the reputation of that force was made on their kindness and their humanity rather than on the well-known cliche that "they always get their man". About 80 per cent of a good policeman's work consists in the prevention of crime. This is done to a great extent by example and by a humane attitude to the public and especially juveniles.
I can quote one example from my own experience. The police of Ontario, the mounted police and the local police combined at the industrial school at Alfred, Ontario to set up a hobby club and a policemen's day and they went to that institution to show friendship to those boys. Within a year the authorities there asserted that juvenile

delinquency, bad manners and bad attitudes to discipline in the school had improved 50 per cent. As soon as these boys began to respect the law enforcement officers their whole attitude to the breaking of the law changed. As I said before, the authorities of that school asserted that there was a 50 per cent improvement in those children in the short space of one year.
I can give another example. In the city of Hamilton some ten years ago a very forward-looking police officer started backyard baseball. This officer was hired at the rate of $7,000 a year by the city of Hamilton. In one year after he started this backyard baseball club the city of Hamilton saved $7,000 in broken glass alone or I should say in the non-breaking of glass alone.
I assert that this is a positive attitude to punishment. I think it can be carried right down through our Criminal Code. There is nothing to be gained by corporal punishment. It is revolting to him who administers it, it is debasing to him who receives it and, wherever it is used, it justifies to the criminal his attitude toward a society in which he feels he has no real part. Unless we can show this criminal-who is after all not greatly different from most of us-that he has a proper place in society; that he is welcome in society; nay, that he is loved by his fellow man, the job of rehabilitating him, once he has been in trouble, is hopeless.
Here is one simple way of showing that we have come out of the jungle, that we no longer look upon him as a wild animal or as an enemy but as a man who has not lived up to the high calling of a dignified human being. I cannot see any argument in favour of using these cruel, outmoded physical tortures in order to try to teach him something different. I should just like to close my few remarks by reminding you, Mr. Speaker, of that great piece in Shakespeare from "The Merchant of Venice" where Portia says:
The quality of mercy is not strain'd.
It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven,
Upon the place beneath. It is twice bless'd:
It blesseth him that gives and him that takes.
If you just draw the parallel and put in the word "punishment" there I think you will see what I mean. Corporal punishment debases him that gives and it certainly debases him that takes.
Once again I should like to add what small weight I can to this argument for doing away with something which is unworthy of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in supporting the bill moved by the hon. member for

York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee). I must also commend him for the work he has put in for some time now, for the purpose of having corporal punishment abolished.
I also would like to commend the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who has also worked hard and long to obtain abolition of corporal punishment. In a speech he made in this house last April he reported that he had visited penitentiaries and had put questions to prisoners who had been subjected to the lash. I should like to quote his own words so that hon. members may realize what cruelty is wrought upon those who are condemned to corporal punishment. The hon. member said-and I quote from page 2317 of the official record of this house for April 7, 1959:
-the warden of the penitentiary has to carry out that order. . . . the inmate is taken into a small room. If it is the lash, there is a table sloping at a 30 degree angle up against the wall. At the end of that table embedded in the concrete are steel plates. The feet of the inmate are fastened by leather straps to the steel plates in the concrete so that he cannot move. He is then stretched along the inclined board, with arms extended, and his arms are strapped to the board so as to be completely immovable. He is stripped to the waist. . . . may I tell you that a leather belt is put around the kidneys because a blow on the kidneys can kill. Then the man who is strapped there, his feet on the floor, his arms extended, with protection so that he cannot be killed, with a leather belt over the kidneys, gets in Canada what is known as the lash.
The hon. member for Vancouver East personally visited, in the hospital, one of the men who had undergone this punishment, and reported that the victim's back was still sore from the lash seven days later.
To my mind, the practice of so barbarous a chastisement, in a civilized country, is a disgrace. The imposition of such punishment is also degrading for the person who has to carry it out. In my view, that type of punishment serves no purpose but that of revenge.
If we look up the various sections of the Criminal Code dealing with offences for which the lash is to be applied, we note, for instance, section 289 which deals with robbery. Now, as an hon. member said this afternoon, out of a total of 700 to 900 cases, the lash was applied in only 1 per cent of those cases. We are forced to the conclusion that the judges were too humane to condemn the others under that section.
Under certain sections of the Criminal Code, the penalty may call for both life imprisonment and the lash.
If the purpose of such a sentence was indeed to reform the guilty, he would not be condemned to the lash, for how can one 66968-9-369i
Criminal Code
expect to reform a criminal who is under a life sentence? That goes to prove, in my opinion, that it is primarily for purposes of revenge that the lash is made part of the sentence.
In my opinion, if the object sought is to reform a criminal, he should be condemned either to prison, or to the lash, but not to both. If it is considered proper to order the lash, the culprit should then be freed immediately after. If the lash was likely to reform a culprit, it could be applied; but it will be seen in several sections of the Criminal Code that the punishment provides up to 14 years of imprisonment, in addition to the lash.
I believe it is a disgrace too for those who have to apply the lash, because their humane feelings are aroused. If the man who carries out the sentence is very humane, he will not use much force; he will try to apply it as humanely as possible, and it is all to his credit. However, in doing so, he might not abide strictly by the requirements of the law. On the other hand, if the man wielding the lash is an inhuman wretch, he will use all his might and apply the lash with cruelty, which would certainly not be a civilized way of applying the punishment.
Especially because the lash can be administered with cruelty, I believe we should react against those methods, we who sit in this parliament and have the authority necessary to amend the sections of the Criminal Code. We should therefore neglect no opportunity to have the corporal punishment abolished.
Once again, I congratulate the mover of the bill and, having done so, I resume my seat, knowing that others are anxious to express their views on the matter.

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes left at my disposal I would like to endorse what was previously said by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg). Certainly it is refreshing to hear him state in the house the principles by which the police act in dealing with offenders against the law. As has been said, many people have the feeling that when the mounted police went out to get their men, not only did they catch them and bring them to justice but they prosecuted them to the fullest extent. I think a good many people do have that feeling. It may never have been felt that was the case with the mounted police, but I know at times the public does have the feeling that the police generally are prosecutors rather than concerning themselves with simply bringing people to justice.

Criminal Code
As has been said, the most important part of the rehabilitation of a person who has got himself into difficulty concerns his selfrespect. I was privileged for five years to do some work in connection with the juvenile court, and during that time I think that was the main lesson I learned. In most cases I found that people who broke the law, people who went out to do malicious damage, were trying to draw attention to themselves for some wrong that they felt had been done to them. It is oversimplification to refer to the sort of person who throws a brick through a window for the sole purpose of being noticed and being brought to justice; but nevertheless such is the case. It is especially noticeable in juveniles, yet I feel that a lot of people who get into difficulty in adulthood are to a large extent just overgrown juveniles and have never got out of that state.
However, the question remains, Mr. Speaker, whether corporal punishment can be dispensed with in all cases. There are those who appear to be hopeless and there are those who are hopeless, and I think that no person who deals in social work or criminology will say everybody can be put back into society as a good member. There are those who time and again are brought before the courts, are sentenced, serve their time, get out and go right back to the same thing. In some cases it is weakness, and I think that in a case like that we should not inflict corporal punishment.
But what about the person who inflicts what we call a heinous crime or inflicts brutal punishment upon another and who does it not only once but several times? I think that we have to consider very seriously how far we may go in connection with a person like that. It has certainly been established that the purpose of punishment is not primarily revenge; it is rehabilitation.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at five o'clock I was pointing out the large returns that we received for money spent in tourist advertising and publicity. I want to put just one more figure on the record before coming to the matter that is of primary concern to me. For every dollar spent on advertising in the United States by this country, $130 in United States currency comes back to Canada in tourist revenue. I do not hesitate to say that for every future dollar that we spend in the same way, a similar return will come back to this country.
I am now through with figures and should like to indicate to the committee why I am so particularly interested and concerned about the tourist business this year. There are three specific reasons. First, even with a general increase in revenues across the board in 1958 in most departments, the income from tourist spending declined about 3 per cent of $11 million. The second reason is that many other countries of the world have concentrated on their tourist business and as a result have reaped great benefits in their garnering of United States dollars. Unfortunately this represents a loss for us in revenue from our traditional market, the United States. People who formerly travelled here are being invited by very high pressure advertising, publicity and travel offices in the United States to travel elsewhere than in Canada.
The third and most serious reason is that next year, 1960, has been declared "Visit U.S.A. 1960" year. This is an undertaking that has been in the course of preparation for several years. It has the personal backing of the President of the United States. It is a concentrated effort by the tourist industry and by the people of the United States to persuade their people first, to travel at home; that is in their own state; second, to bring people to the United States from other

countries as extensively as they can; and, third, to encourage inter-state travel within the United States. This can have a devastating effect on Canada's 1960 tourist industry if we do not immediately take steps to counteract it.
"Visit U.S.A. 1960" has an eight-point program. I do not want to give it any more publicity than it should have but I do wish to point out what we in Canada are going to have to meet next year. The reason I am doing so is that 1959 is our last chance to persuade the visitors to Canada this year to return next year. Already some of the large 1960 conventions arranged for major cities in Canada, particularly Montreal, have been cancelled. Certain people in the United States will consider it their patriotic duty to hold their conventions at home next year. That is only a start in early 1959, and other results will be forthcoming. For that reason I believe we must be very concerned about this United States undertaking. The greater part of our travel industry originates from the United States and we do not want to lose a large percentage of our market through United States people being persuaded to travel at home in 1960 and in the future.
I wish to set out six of the eight points of the United States program as being illustrative of what we will have to meet. They are contained in a newsletter published by the Curtis Publishing Company of Washington, D.C., publishers of Holiday magazine. The letter is dated July 2, 1959. The following will give us an idea of the lines along which their program is being conducted:
1.	Urge each state and territory to encourage travel within its borders both by visitors from abroad and from other parts of the United States.
2.	Urge cities to attract visitors during the period, set up suitable municipal travel information centres, and encourage foreign nationality groups within their confines to assist with the program.
3.	Urge corporations and trade and service organizations with operations abroad to use the "Visit U.S.A. I960" theme in their advertising and promotional activities, as well as to encourage their representatives in foreign countries to visit the United States in 1960.
4.	Support legislation to repeal the 10 per cent excise tax on the transportation of foreign persons within the United States.
5.	Urge continued negotiations by the United States government with other governments to ease currency restrictions which deter pleasure travel to the United States.
6.	Urge government agencies with jurisdiction over recreational areas, national shrines and points of interest to visitors to make available before and during 1960 more adequate supplies of informational material.
A good many of those points could very well be applied to Canada, but it is too late now for us to counter this move except by immediate action. I am not saying that this is entirely the responsibility of government.
Supply-Northern Affairs At this late stage in 1959 I doubt if there is much the government could do except encourage and support our own industry. It is the responsibility of tourist operators themselves and of the public in Canada generally to welcome their visitors this year, to give them good service, good meals and good accommodations, and to extend such courtesy that these visitors will want to return to Canada in 1960 and bring guests, or send their friends.
In the committee on mines, forests and waters we learned that 40 per cent of the people who come to Canada as visitors come here because of something they have heard from someone else. Word-of-mouth advertising is the most immediate and important medium. We must embark upon a program of this nature. Our visitors must have some reason to come back. As I say, this summer season is our last chance to undertake this program.
We in Canada this year must bend our efforts to making our tourist season the most significant one we have had. I am very happy to say that in the area I represent, Parry Sound-Muskoka, which to a large extent is a tourist area, the picture is very bright this year. Summer came early and hot weather always drives people out of the city and into the country. The visit of Her Majesty and Prince Philip created much interest and brought many visitors to Canada early. We are off to a good start this year. I wish to appeal to all the people in Canada who are coming in contact with tourists to make it their special job this year to extend courtesy to their guests.
It may be asked what the government can do. I am not going to deal with that now because this subject was well covered in the last report of the committee on mines, forests and waters under the vote relating to the Canadian government travel bureau. In that report there are some excellent suggestions which if carried out would be of vast assistance. I leave it at that. Many answers to our problems are contained in that report.
