speechtext:
My hon. friend said "in spite of the Liberal party". It is a great tribute to the people of Canada, of course, that they could have had this amazing period of development, according to my hon. friend, in spite of the Liberal party. The truth is that the Liberal government of those days provided the framework of policy within which -and this is all we ever claimed-this amazing period of development occurred.
The minister, of course, sometimes in the exuberance of his vision, mistakes propaganda for performance. For instance, this afternoon he talked about the Columbia river development as if that was something that began in June, 1957; whereas he knows the present government is carrying on-I hope to successful completion-the important plans for this development which were initiated several years ago.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, we all know that the planning and development of a nation like Canada, especially perhaps of a nation like Canada, require vision. Had there not been vision since 1867 in this country, and not merely since 1957, Canada would not have reached the position she has reached today, and therefore vision is required, but planning and development require more than vision. It requires a realistic and sober appreciation of resources and means. It must not become a development where those who are responsible for government become so dazzled by the distant scene that they stumble or ignore the steps to be taken immediately ahead. That is our criticism of so much that the government has done and is doing. For instance, the minister may remember the great vision of a third transcontinental railway. The effort to realize that vision prematurely did not help in Canada's development; it hindered Canada's development and we are paying for that premature vision at the present time.

The realization of our national development through planning has to be brought about step by step without timidity, of course, but also without rashness; with common sense as well as with dazzling optimism and within our economic resources; with regard, of course, to a particular area of the country which is going to benefit by any particular scheme, naturally, but also with regard to the effect on the nation as a whole of any plan for any particular area.
Of course, the minister pays special attention to the north and no one has any right to complain about that. It is well in this country that we should pay special attention not only to what is perhaps Canada's last frontier but in a sense perhaps the world's most important frontier. Considerations that make this last frontier important are not only commercial, not only economic, but are considerations of defence and strategy, considerations of our relations with the United States of America and considerations of our relations with the Soviet union. Sometimes we get impatient in this country and sometimes there is complaint because we have not been able to develop our Arctic areas as speedily and as sensationally as they have in the Soviet union. We forget that we are 17J millions of people; the Russians are 200 millions of people. We forget sometimes that we are a free society and that we have to persuade, induce through incentives, people to go north while the Russians can order any number of people to go north to do anything they want them to do.
There is something else about national development that we occasionally forget, and I ventured to mention this in the last session, namely that national development is not merely the opening up of new areas in our country. It can also take the form of assistance in the re-development of older areas. There is a great deal to do in this country in that respect in some of those areas which have not shared to the full, as they have the right to expect, in the economic development of our country. Perhaps that kind of national development is not as glamorous as looking ahead to arrange for submarines to sail with oil under the Arctic ice, or building glass palaces at Frobisher; but it can be even more important to the country as a whole. However, as I have said, I have no complaint with the minister's concentration on the north, with his vision of development in the north, but I do, complain, Mr. Chairman, about exaggerations and distortions and indeed the falsification of that particular vision.
I am thinking particularly of a subject which has occupied this house for a good deal of time this session already, and concerning which there has been discussion both

in the house and before the appropriate committee, namely the question of permit rights and applications for gas and oil licences in northern Canada, and in particular an attempt by the Prime Minister, the minister and at least one of his colleagues, to associate that development with claims for the protection of our sovereignty in the area against the encroachment of the United States; in contrast with the situation which existed before 1957. In particular there is the contention of the Prime Minister that the granting of those rights has been a major means of preserving the sovereignty of Canada by the present government in those northern areas. I would like to begin by quoting again what I put on the record of the house on March 9, namely a television broadcast of the Prime Minister on the nation's business, one paragraph of which reads:
It was because I knew Canadians felt so strongly about the necessity of preserving Canada's destiny that I have advocated and the government has launched its national development policy to push back our northern frontiers. The result of our action has been that in the last several weeks-
This was in March, 1959.
-over 75 million acres in northern Canada have been taken up for oil and mineral development, and I want to underline this that this is a major means to preserve our sovereignty.
The expressions used by the Prime Minister that I would emphasize are, first, "in northern Canada" and, second, "taken up for oil and mineral development". We also noticed at the time that he used the figure of 75 million acres. It was perfectly natural to connect that figure of 75 million acres used by the Prime Minister in that particular broadcast with the statement made earlier in the house by the minister on February 13 when the minister said, and I quote from page 995 of Hansard:
I should like to emphasize to the house that this is in addition to the 76 million acres-
The Prime Minister had said "over 75 million".
-now under permit in the mainland of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
The minister was referring to 76 million acres on the mainland of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon which presumably was the area which the Prime Minister was referring to when he talked about almost 76 million acres. Then, on March 10 of this year the minister on his own initiative made a statement in the House of Commons in connection with the public sale of oil and gas permits in northern Canada for 3,546,829 acres. The minister had this to say on March 10 as found on page 1774 of Hansard:
Supply-Northern Affairs
All the acreage, except for some 250,000 acres, lies in the southwestern Northwest Territories and southeastern Yukon in the general vicinity of Fort Liard.
That reference was to the sale of oil and gas permits in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon territory, not, I point out, to the Arctic islands at all. The minister also made the following statement on that occasion:
I should emphasize that this sale is for exploratory privileges only, though if the permittee complies with the regulations he may acquire up to 50 percent of each area as an oil and gas lease. He must apply for such a lease if he discovers oil and gas and wishes to commence production.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, the issue of a permit has certain obligations and gives certain privileges. In view of the Prime Minister's statement made the preceding evening on a national network I asked the minister when he finished that statement how many of the bids he mentioned were made by United States corporations or Canadian subsidiaries of such corporations because the Prime Minister had made such a point about the preservation of Canadian sovereignty in this way. Later in answer to a question by the hon. member for Mackenzie River the minister provided the percentage acreage which showed that for that particular sale of something over three million acres on March 9 Canadian corporations held only 4 per cent and United States corporations and Canadian subsidiaries of United States corporations held 93 per cent of the acreage under permit in that particular sale of something over three million acres.
It was certainly clear that in so far as this particular sale was concerned there was very little done to enhance or protect Canadian sovereignty because of the fact that 93 per cent of these permits went to United States corporations or Canadian subsidiaries. I made reference to this fact in my speech in the house on April 21 and the minister and some of his colleagues took violent exception to the way I put it. They said I was misrepresenting the situation because I was giving the impression that these percentages applied to the 75 million acres. I admit that certainly was an impression that could have been taken and so when they made their complaints, as found on page 2911 of Hansard, I corrected myself and I mentioned that this particular sale applied only to the parcel of land in question of something over three million acres.
However, in the light of the minister's violent, and it was violent, intervention on that occasion we on this side decided to seek from him information with respect to the whole of the northern area of which the minister had provided us with information for only one sale, that on March 9. For that

Supply-Northern Affairs reason the hon. member for Ottawa West asked a further question, the answer to which will be found in Hansard for April 29, page 3148. The question read as follows:
1.	Were 75 million acres recently taken up in northern Canada for oil and mineral development?
2.	If so, by whom?
3.	What percentage has been assigned to (a) Canadian corporations; (b) United States corporations and Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies; (c) British corporations; (d) others?
The minister replied to that question in a most peculiar manner. He threw up quite a smokecreen to conceal the actual facts. In fact, he shifted the discussion. Whether he threw up this smokescreen for that purpose I do not know. Perhaps I should not say he did it for that purpose but that certainly was the effect of the answer he gave because he shifted the discussion from the subject which had been under discussion up to that point, namely permit rights on the mainland-that is what we were talking about-to applications for exploratory licences in the Arctic islands. On the basis of such applications for exploratory licences in the Arctic islands, which had nothing to do with the question at all, and not on the basis of permits granted, which was the question, not even on the basis of applications granted, the minister was able to show to the house and to the country that 68 per cent of the 86 million acres for which applications had been made consisted of Canadian applications.
The minister is pretty naive if he thinks he can get away with such an obvious effort to confuse the discussion and to mislead the opposition in that way in a matter which is of such importance in view of what the Prime Minister and the minister himself had been saying about it outside the house. So, in awareness of this particular technique and after a very strange speech indeed by the Prime Minister in Montreal which I will deal with a little later, the hon. member for Mackenzie River put a further question on the order paper which was answered on May 20, 1959, page 3836 of Hansard.
In that question the opposition made a further attempt to get information covering all the northern areas on the mainland which the minister accused me of failing to provide in my speech on April 21. So we asked what was the total acreage for which exploratory oil and gas permits were issued, not applications for licences, between July 1, 1957, and March 31, 1959, on the mainland of northern Canada. The Prime Minister had said that there were over 75 million acres for which permits had been granted in his television broadcast in February. The answer given by the minister was that in 21 months, not in recent weeks as the Prime Minister had said,


permits had been issued for 60 million acres on the mainland of northern Canada.
So we now ask the minister how Canadian sovereignty, in the words of the Prime Minister, was preserved by issuing under his jurisdiction in that period permits for 60 million acres on the mainland of Canada.
The answer to that question is quite clear because according to the minister's own figures more than 70 per cent of this total acreage of 60 million acres was granted to non-Canadian companies, a total of 63 per cent to United States corporations or Canadian subsidiaries of United States corporations and less than 30 per cent of the total acreage was granted to Canadian corporations. Now I ask the minister, based on the information given for all the northern areas, all the mainland, based on the figures that were given and not just on the sale of March 9 about which he complained earlier, was he justified in saying that this is a major means of preserving our sovereignty? If it is, then it is less than 30 per cent sovereignty.
In this same answer, which will be found on page 3836 of Hansard if the minister is looking for it, the minister did something else. He tried to produce a figure for both the mainland and the Arctic islands by adding together the permits granted on the mainland and the applications for licences on the islands. He produced, in that strange way, a figure for the whole of the north, the islands and the mainland. Mr. Chairman, that figure was nonsensical and misleading, I would say, because by adding applications to permits- two very different things-he made a total which was just about as sensible as if he had added oranges to apples and got 50 of the former. It is quite true that applications made for the Arctic islands by Canadian individuals and corporations covered 68.74 per cent of the total acreage. As we know, some of these applications were from very unusual sources indeed. However, of the 60 million acres for which permits were granted, less than 30 per cent went to Canadian corporations or Canadian individuals.
The conclusion to be drawn from the additional information provided by the minister is even more damning than the information provided for the sale of March 9 covering only three million acres. The information now shows that while Canadian individuals and Canadian corporations made most of the applications, United States corporations got most of the permits in the Canadian north. The minister, in explaining to the committee how these applications are received and how the permits are granted, has said that there are three categories or stages, as follows: First, there is the application; second, there

is the exploratory licence which is valid for one year and which allows geological reconnaissance; then, third, there is the exploratory permit which imposes obligations, which allows drilling, and later can give rights for leases if the permittee fulfils certain undertakings.
The minister has now given us the acreages for the Arctic islands and the continental shelf covering applications and nothing else. He has given us the acreages on the mainland relating to exploratory permits. Now, let me talk about the exploratory permits, and we are getting down to business. With all this information before him, with all this information having been made public, it is amazing that the Prime Minister in May would repeat the kind of statement he made over TV. I have his statement here. This was, I think, on May 8. I am quoting from page 10 of the text of the Prime Minister's speech, where he had this to say:
In the far north, as a direct result of action taken by this government 85.9 million acres on the Canadian mainland in the Mackenzie district and the Yukon have been taken up by firms and individuals for oil and gas development.
A few weeks before he had restricted it to 75 million acres, and the minister said the figure was 60 million acres. Now, before this great Conservative dinner in Montreal on May 8 the Prime Minister has a figure of 85.9 million acres as the acreage which he said had been taken up by firms and individuals for oil and gas development and which was apparently meant, if the Prime Minister's words meant anything, to cover exploratory permits whereas, as I have said, the minister in his official figures said only 60 million acres had been given out since July 1, 1957, and of these 60 million acres less than 30 per cent had been given to Canadian companies. Then, the Prime Minister in the next paragraph of his speech had this to say:
Another 86.5 million acres on the continental shelf in the Arctic islands are now being developed under exploratory permits. These are stupendous figures.
They certainly are stupendous, in more ways than one. I continue to quote:
The potential of expansion which they imply for the Canadian economy is almost beyond imagination.
These figures are almost beyond imagination, too, because the Prime Minister said 86.5 million acres were under exploratory permits in the Arctic islands. Not so, says the minister, there are no permits on the Arctic islands, only applications, as I shall be able to prove later by quoting the minister's own words. Then, the Prime Minister went on:
What is equally important in this connection is that Canadians are taking the lead in this
Supply-Northern Affairs
development of Canadian resources. 68.7 per cent of the applications covering these 86.5 million acres are from Canadian corporations and individuals;-
Yet we know that that is true only in respect of applications and is quite wrong in respect of permits granted because 60 per cent or more of those went to the United States. Then, the Prime Minister finished by saying that it is apparent Canadian sovereignty has not been neglected; that Canadians are taking the lead in this matter and Canadian sovereignty this time has not been neglected.
Canadians are taking the lead all right in making the applications because the figures given refer to applications, not to permits. Making applications is hardly the development of Canadian resources. We claim, and the figures given by the minister himself prove it, that the United States is taking the lead in getting exploratory permits and Canadians are taking the lead in making the applications. The Canadians apply and the United States citizens receive. As a result of this, the Prime Minister said that Canadian sovereignty in the Arctic is being protected in this particular way.
In his earlier speech the Prime Minister had said that 75 million acres were taken up recently, and now he gets this figure of 75 million raised by May to 85.9 million acres. What did he mean by "recently" in the earlier speech? We do know, I repeat, that this particular government gave permits for 60 million acres, of which more than 70 per cent went to non-Canadian corporations.
When I stated, as I did a few moments ago, that when the Prime Minister talked about permits being given in the Arctic islands he was contradicted by his own minister, perhaps I had better prove that particular statement. Not only did the minister contradict the Prime Minister, but he has contradicted himself in this matter. Here is what he said to the committee, and I am reading from report No. 14, page 351 of the committee evidence, and this is in respect of the issuing of permits:
A question was asked yesterday in the house by another hon. member which allowed me to state what was happening in the area of the Arctic islands-
Then he went on to say this:
-where there are now 86 million acres under permit.
That is what the minister told the committee. Perhaps that was the basis upon which the Prime Minister made his statement in public. But what did the minister
5824	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs say in the House of Commons? I quote from Hansard of February 13, page 995 as follows:
In the Arctic islands the oil and gas regulations are being revised, and until such time as the revision is complete no permits are being issued.
Then later, just a day before the statement he made to the committee which I have quoted and in which he said there were no permits being issued in the Arctic islands the minister had this to say on April 29, as reported at page 3149 of Hansard:
Very recently, however, interest has been shown in the Arctic islands and in the sea bed and subsoil of the continental shelf off Canada's northern coast. If the hon. member refers to this more recent activity the strict answer to his first question is no, since up to the present no permits have been granted in the Arctic islands or the continental shelf.
Which are we to believe? Are we to believe the minister in the committee, or the minister in the House of Commons? Later, on May 6, just before the Prime Minister spoke in Montreal-in fact two days before the Prime Minister spoke in Montreal-the minister had this to say as reported at page 3377 of Hansard:
These companies simply requested priority to obtain oil and gas permits when the revised oil and gas regulations are promulgated-
The licences issued do not cover a specific acreage but are designed for general geological exploration anywhere in the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory, including the Arctic islands.
In other words, they were not permits at all. Then again on May 11, just after the Prime Minister spoke, the minister as reported at page 3514 of Hansard had this to say. This was after the Prime Minister had made his statement in Montreal.
First of all I would like to make it clear that we have not issued any exploratory permits . . . with regard to the Arctic islands and the continental shelf.
Perhaps the minister, before these discussions end, would try to explain some of these contradictions. If we on this side of the chamber have some doubts as to the reality of the minister's statement with regard to the vision, perhaps contradictory statements of this kind in the house and in public, perhaps this kind of statement of the Prime Minister made about the protection of Canadian sovereignty in the Arctic, give us some justification for having those doubts.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
In view of the obvious sensitivity of the Leader of the Opposition with regard to the terrible fluff that he made in the house some weeks ago on this matter of describing the sovereignty of the north on the basis of one sale of three and a half million acres, I think I should like to clear that record up but fast. I am going


to say frankly to the Leader of the Opposition that if he wants to make use of dialectics in quarrelling over the words "exploratory licences" and permits that are waiting servicing, let him go ahead.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Just tell the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: However, the thing be remembered is this. At no time did the Prime Minister ever make a false statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Read his speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: If the Leader of the Opposition wants to stand up in this house and say that he made a false statement, let him stand up and say so.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Those are dialectics.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: All the hon. member does is to comfort himself by saying that at one time the Prime Minister spoke of 75 million acres, another time I spoke of 60 million acres, another time the Prime Minister spoke of 85 million acres or 85.9 million acres, to be accurate, and another time he spoke of 86.5 million acres. Let me explain this to the Leader of the Opposition. Right tonight, July 10, the number of acres that are out under application for permits in the Arctic island is 95.4 million acres.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: How many permits have been issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: When I make this statement I expect the Leader of the Opposition to go up and down the country and to say that I have contradicted myself. The only thing he cannot stomach is the fact that business people from all countries are taking an interest in our resources and these applications for permits are coming in every day. That is the thing that he cannot stomach.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Why don't you tell the truth?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: His advisers told him in 1958 that all this program was a program from igloo to igloo, and he has lived to regret it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Why don't you answer with facts?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
That facts are as I have given them here now. Up to the period of 1957 there were in the Yukon two reservations of roughly 6 million acres. A recent figure is 6,133,760 acres. This was by reservation. In addition, up to July 1, 1957 there were 18,794,504 acres given out before this government changed.

This was over a long period of time and some of these permits for exploration are now running out. After the change of government there was an obvious increase in interest which was shown particularly in the fall of 1957; and during that period on the mainland and to the present time-up to roughly about three weeks ago when these figures were compiled-the figure had risen to the figure quoted by the Leader of the Opposition. On the mainland in addition to the reservation of permits before July, 1957, an additional 60,942,006 acres were given out. Then starting last February there was a rush on the islands off the shores of our mainland covering some continental shelf and covering these islands and this figure in this tabulation I have here, is shown at 89,018,364 acres. The most recent figure to date, the total in the Arctic islands now under application for permits is now 95,451,508 acres. The total in the Arctic islands under application for permits is now 95,451,508 acres. Those figures will change day by day. Therefore every time I give up to date figures I suppose I contradict myself.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Give the exploration permits.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Does the minister not know the difference between an application and a permit?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition made a great play over this difference between applications for permits and permits. I want to assure this committee that as far as the development of resources is concerned-and his own words were that applications are hardly the development of Canadian resources-at this very moment there are-and I am just trying to check the figures-either 10 companies or 12 companies actively engaged in work in these northern islands under these applications for permits and such work is just as useful for the development of resources whether it is done under application for permit or under actual permit.
What was the reason why we let them have these exploratory licences or to work, as I call it, under application for a permit? The reason was simple. To any person knowing the difficulties in the northern islands it was obvious that there had to be promulgated a set of regulations that would meet the conditions there; first of all to encourage companes to go into this area and, second, to make sure that the resources there were effectively administered and used in the best interest of this country. We were therefore working on these regulations last fall with no expectation that this rush would suddenly break out in February. When the rush actually did break out we drafted quickly a series of regulations and intended to put them into
Supply-Northern Affairs effect. The government has been studying these regulations with the idea of seeing that everything is done not only to protect the utilization of these resources in the best interests of the people of Canada, but to make sure, as far as we can go, that there is effective administration by the Canadian people of these resources.
Mr. Chairman, a great deal of play has been made over these percentage figures. I have been quite candid with the percentage going to Canadian companies, the percentage going to Canadian subsidiaries, to United States companies, British companies, Dutch companies, French companies, to other foreign companies, and the percentage going to United States or Canadian individuals. These percentages do not mean anything in the long run.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Why give them then?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
What does
mean something is who has the oil and gas when it is found? I heard from the hon, member for Bonavista-Twillingate the expression, "Why give them?" The answer is is that I was not the person who asked for these percentages; they were asked for by the Leader of the Opposition, and all across this country went a headline that 93 per cent of our northern oil and gas lands had got into the hands of United States companies.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Who said that?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: That was a statement of the press.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Quote a headline.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: In the Canadian Press. I stood up on a point of order that night and tried to correct the Leader of the Opposition, and my correction was not allowed. He kept going on and on, and finally Mr. Speaker had to let me have two minutes before the vote was taken to try to correct the Leader of the Opposition. Now he comes along tonight, on July 10, several months after this occasion, and admits he is wrong.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I would like to call the minister's attention to page 2911 of Hansard for April 21, where I said:
-we get specific information covering about three million acres, we find that 95 per cent of these leases were granted to United States corporations-
I made that statement after the minister corrected me.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: That is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand how sensitive the Leader of the Opposition is, because when a person has

Supply-Northern Affairs made a horrible blunder of the calibre the Leader of the Opposition made I can understand him trying to get out of it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: But it is apparent to the people of Canada that the hon. member has a great deal to learn about domestic problems in this country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: It is also apparent, too, to this house that we have been very patient while the Leader of the Opposition tries to learn something about what goes on in Canada. I can see from the annoyance of the hon. members across the way that they are not too happy about the fact that with regard to the oil and gas development in the north there is, or rather was up until a few weeks ago because the figures are higher now, a total of 168,754,876 acres out under permits for exploration and exploratory licences, or, if you want to be more accurate, applications for permits.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Yes; be accurate, that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: I am accurate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Be honest.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
In addition
there is this reservation of six million acres, and to be even more accurate, Mr. Chairman, with regard to waters under territorial lands there is the additional seven million acres out under permits or applications for permits at the present time. I think the Canadian people will be satisfied with this work which is going on, and I want to conclude my remarks with what the Leader of the Opposition has said on this salient point of sovereignty. If the Leader of the Opposition goes back-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: It was the Prime Minister who talked about sovereignty.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Let us be accurate.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: -knows that he can make a speech any time he likes on my estimates.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: And he will.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: I wish he would let me finish this topic, because I know he will wish he had not interjected.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Coming back to this salient question of sovereignty, in my opinion there is no question of sovereignty on any part of the mainland of Canada; but there is a small question of doubt in the


minds of some who are unaware of the facts about our sovereignty on the Arctic islands and the areas around them. Therefore this is, if I may use the word "sensitive" in the correct way, a sensitive area for Canada, and if the Leader of the Opposition goes back to the discussion of the estimates last year he will find out that he agreed that the only way we could maintain sovereignty in our far northern areas was by effective occupation. That is not my phrase. It is not his phrase. But we both agreed that this was the effective way, and I think that he would be fair enough to admit that the most effective occupation that Canada can provide is effective, tangible administration. Whether it be the operation of airfields or D.E.W. line stations or weather stations or the new airfields we are constructing in the islands or the research teams we have there or the company activities looking for oil and gas, so long as that is done under our effective administration, that is the most tangible evidence to any person in any part of the world that this is Canada and that this is the land we will fight for.
I hope I have said enough to answer the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, and I think that he should join with us and be proud that this development has taken place. I know that the development of these northern areas will take a long time, but I believe, not only in theory but in fact, that the most realistic way to do it is to approach our undeveloped territories from the south up through the provinces and through the east and north at the same time in a vast pincer movement. It is very important to us as a nation to make certain that with submarines going around the Arctic seas this area is beyond question the sovereign area of Canada, and this oil and gas exploration in the northern areas has come as a great boon to us. We are rather happy that in the figures I have quoted in answer to one of the questions the percentage in the Arctic islands at that date, of Canadian companies or Canadian individuals who held licences was 68 per cent. At the present time the percentage is a little higher. I know, as I said earlier, that percentages do not mean anything. It is who has the oil in the end that counts, after all. But as far as sovereignty is concerned, as long as that company is working under our direction, then by effective administration of that resource in that area we are giving the best evidence of sovereignty that we can give. If more Canadian individuals and more Canadian companies and more Canadian subsidiaries of foreign companies get this acreage than outside companies, it will make us all a little more nationally conscious that Canadians are getting up there and getting their share.

As a matter of fact, I think the committee would like to know what the percentages are over this whole area. I will be very careful here. I am now quoting from the document I have before me which goes back two or three weeks to the time of the committee. These are the percentages on the mainland and on the islands, and they include permits and applications for permits, because in our minds, and in the mind of any person who is sensible, when these applications go in the permits are taken out and it is in effect the same thing. If one or two dropped out it would not seriously affect the figures. At the present time, over the whole north-

speechtext: Before the minister starts on that, would he permit one question?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Could the minister say
whether every one of these applicants is going to be given a permit?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I must say I was very pleased to hear the minister's response to the very constructive proposals made by the unassuming but hardworking hon. member for Mackenzie. 1 know the member has long thought of those questions that he brought before the committee this afternoon and indeed, in listening to his speech, I thought he made a very comprehensive and constructive approach to the questions with which he dealt.
As a backwoodsman who has had an interest in forest conservation for 50 years, and who happened to be a forest farmer during that whole period, I am going to confine my remarks entirely to the forestry section of the report of the committee on mines, forests and waters. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that during my whole life I have had four major affections and interests: the first, the ladies; the second, trees; the third, horses; and the fourth, ships; but this evening I am going to deal with the question of trees-

speechtext:
-first of all, because of my particular interest in this question over practically my whole life time, and because of the fact that 40 per cent of the production of the province from which I come, British Columbia, results from the forest industry.
We have made considerable progress since the second world war. I remember before the Canada Forestry Act was passed there were representations, in the first instance I am very proud to say, from the representatives of the forest industry in British Columbia urging that such an act be passed by the federal government, and representations from the Canadian Forestry Association and the Canadian Institute of Forestry. That was the first, shall I say, great step so far as the federal government was concerned with respect to legislation which provided for cooperation between the federal and the various provincial governments. Since that act was passed there has been a great deal of good accomplished. Forest inventories have been undertaken in the various provinces as a result of the agreements, and I understand that most of those are practically completed. There has been work undertaken with respect to reforestation as a result of agreements between the federal and provincial governments and some very effective work undertaken as a result of agreements with respect to forest fire protection and some limited work undertaken as a result of agreements with respect to aerial spraying projects.
Also, since the passing of the Canada Forestry Act, there has been considerable

Supply-Northern Affairs extension of the research work undertaken by the forestry branch of the minister's department and also quite an advance in education. But, as the minister mentioned previously this afternoon, for 25 years the committee on mines, forests and waters had not met. I had the honour of being a member of this committee from 1945 to 1957, a committee which never met during that whole period. However, I must say that the question of the necessity for the committee meeting and the other questions related to further interest required on the part of the federal government in forestry projects were kept alive by the Canadian Forestry Association, the Canadian Institute of Foresters and various conservation organizations across this country.
I cannot pass by this aspect of the question without referring to the excellent work done by the British Columbia natural resources conference which was established in the first instance, I think in 1949, under the coalition government of British Columbia at that time. There is no other province in Canada that has undertaken a series of annual conferences of' this type which have contributed a great deal toward an understanding of the problems with respect to the innumerable natural resources in the province of British Columbia.
I notice while I am speaking that my colleague from Port Arthur is mumbling and growling because I am making some complimentary references with respect to what we do in British Columbia, but I shall not take any notice of him. I want to tell hon. members on behalf of the C.C.F. group that we discuss these questions in our caucus. We have urged a number of things. I might say I am very delighted with the report that the committee on mines, forests and waters had presented to this house, and in particular with respect to the forestry section of the minister's department.
For years I urged that the committee on mines, forests and waters meet and that the estimates of the minister's department be referred to that committee, without result. My pleas fell on deaf ears. I am very glad to know that since the minister has taken office the committee on mines, forests and waters met in 1958 and again this year. I just want to mention that because it indicates that there is an influence from the C.C.F. group in this house throughout the years. It is the eroding of the hard stone, but we do find that we accomplish our objectives.
For some 12 years I have urged the necessity of a dominion-provincial conference to deal with the question of a national policy for the conservation of land, forests, water and other renewable natural resources. Year after year this question has been discussed

in the house on a private member's resolution introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay West on behalf of the C.C.F. group. I was very pleased at that time, when I introduced the resolution and there was an opportunity to debate it, that it was supported by the Progressive Conservative members on the opposition side of the house during those years. I am very glad to note that our efforts in that respect have brought some results. In that connection I want to put an editorial from the Lethbridge Herald of December 1, 1958, on the record because I was very pleased indeed to read this. The heading is, "Conservation Study", and it reads as follows:
A meeting of federal and provincial representatives held in Ottawa in mid-November has gone almost unnoticed, though it may turn out to have been one of the most important in a decade. For it reached agreement on the holding, no later than the summer of 1960, of a national conference on conservation "to discuss the multiple use of such renewable natural resources as soil, forests, wildlife, fish, water and recreational facilities".
Conservation has had but half-hearted treatment in this country to date. Organizations like the Canadian forestry association and fish and game associations have long been active within their respective fields, and in recent years governments have taken preliminary steps to ensure the wise use of our renewable resources. But in no province, so far as we know, have conservation measures been either co-ordinated or adequately planned, and interprovincial and federal-provincial co-operation have been negligible.
There is no guarantee, to be sure, that the national conference on conservation will utter the last words on the subject. But judging by its aims, it should bring some worthwhile improvements. Those aims are:	(1) Assembling information on
the present status of resource management and research in Canada. (A steering committee to be set up shortly to compile material from provincial governments and other agencies on resource activities.)
(2)	Discussing weaknesses and gaps in the field of resource management and research.
(3)	Indicating areas where further efforts are required.
(4)	Creating a better understanding on the part of the public at large, governments and industrial and other special groups of the meaning of conservation, its present status in Canada and its implications for the future.
The very fact that conservation is to be examined at the federal-provincial level is a happy augury. We congratulate the Diefenbaker government for initiating this development; and we think praise is also due to Mr. H. W. Herridge, M.P. for Kootenay West, who over many years has been a persistent advocate of just such a move as this.
I could not resist reading that editorial, Mr. Chairman, because although my pleas fell on deaf ears in the case of the former Liberal government I am delighted that finally the present government has taken action in that respect because I think it is a most important subject and I look forward to some very excellent results from this conference.

Another thing that I want to urge on behalf of the C.C.F. group is the necessity for the establishment of a department of forestry separate from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I am delighted, Mr. Chairman, to know that the committee has recommended exactly that, following right in our trail. Once again the C.C.F. has indicated that it thinks well in advance and that its policies are sound.
Then I have urged for years on behalf of this group the necessity of an increase in the money appropriated for research, the necessity of the expansion of research with respect to our forest products laboratories and research in the field. I am therefore pleased to note that in the committee's report it recommends that very thing, the expansion of research so far as the forestry branch is concerned.
Then again, for some 12 years I have urged on behalf of this group the point of view that there should be a review of taxation policies with respect to federal government and provincial government taxation. I have urged for years that there should be similar consideration given to the forest industry, the lumber industry and the pulp and paper industry, with respect to exemptions for roads, firefighting equipment, trails, telephones and all these extra costs associated with development, as is given at the present time to the mining, gas and oil industries.

Then again, on behalf of this group I have urged the necessity for expansion of access trails and roads to make possible the more efficient fighting of fires in the forests of Canada, and I am very pleased to notice that the committee has recommended exactly that. In that connection, as the evidence before the committee will show, we have the heads of the great firm of MacMillan, Bloedel and Stewart, other representatives of the forest industry of British Columbia, the Vancouver board of trade, all the trade unions of British Columbia, in fact, all the sensible people of British Columbia, supporting this policy at this time. These things that I have advocated on behalf of this group have not been advocated out of thin air. They are the result of discussion and consideration. Every one of these policies that have been advocated over a period of 13 years by the member for Kootenay West on behalf of this group has received the support of the entire forest industry of British Columbia and the trade union organizations associated with it.
I do want to say Mr. Chairman, that this excellent report of the committee clearly indicates a lack of action on the part of the government of Canada, action that should have been taken before now. I must say that I was very pleased to hear the minister say that he gave his officials carte blanche to answer freely the questions asked by the committee. It is quite evident from the report that the committee has made to the house that the committee has not been under any duress or pressure whatever from the minister or the government to restrict or modify its report. I am very pleased to note that. Mind you, it is a very forward looking report and possibly contains some things that will give the minister headaches in future months or years, but I think it is a genuinely democratic report that expresses the opinions of the members of the committee.
I may say that I was not a member of the committee but I was allowed to sit in when forestry was under consideration and have my little say from time to time. I appreciate very much the kindness of the committee in that respect. This report is a democratic report from a committee without any strings attached which offers a great opportunity to the minister and the government in the days ahead.
Before concluding I do want to urge on the basis of this report that the minister give consideration to further amendments to the Canada Forestry Act which are required if the act is going to function satisfactorily under present conditions. I think that the report offers a sound basis for amendments to that act. The national conference proposed by the minister not later than 1960 offers a very sound basis for the government to take the lead to write the first dominion-provincial charter for dominion-provincial co-operation with respect to the conservation, utilization and development of our natural resources.
Before I sit down I want to say a few words with respect to the staff. We are most fortunate in the staff at present employed in the minister's department and the high standard of their academic qualifications and experience. Anyone who knows anything about the forest industry will know that they

Supply-Northern Affairs are not receiving the salaries they should. In a company with which I am acquainted there is one forest engineer who gets almost as much salary as the deputy minister of the department. Private industry is offering much larger salaries to this type of official than is being offered by the federal government. Provincial governments are offering much larger salaries than are being offered by the federal government.
As an illustration, I may say that the premier of British Columbia went out and, unrestricted by a civil service act or other regulations which are some restriction upon the minister and other members of his government, simply offered Mr. Keenleyside $25,000 a year to come and take over a position with the British Columbia power commission. That sounds like a lot of money. However, the premier of British Columbia was smart in doing that. He picked up a first class man with great capacity, academic qualifications and great experience and secured his services for the British Columbia power commission. Unfortunately, our federal ministers cannot do the same sort of thing. They are restricted by the Civil Service Act, the treasury board, regulations and so on. I do suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if we are going to maintain the services of this type of qualified people, some of whom have given long and devoted service to this and other departments of government, and if we are going to get the best of the younger people who are coming along, then the government should give consideration to changing its salary schedules in the very near future.
It is not fair to expect men with high qualifications and experience to continue serving the government of Canada and the people of Canada for salaries which, in some cases, are about 50 per cent of what these same people could obtain with provincial governments or in private industry. I do urge, Mr. Chairman, that the government give consideration to this problem so that we can retain the excellent staff we have at the present time, and can recruit the services of the brighter young men who are coming forward to take their part in the government service of the future.

I should like to make a few brief comments here with regard to the statement made by the Prime Minister on June 4 regarding the appointment of the personnel of a board to inquire into and report upon the respective merits of the alternative routes which might be followed by a railway line to be built from northern Alberta, and so on. I am just reciting part of the terms of reference. I was most happy to hear of this


announcement because it seems to me that it was the only thing to do under all the complicated circumstances which surround the program. It also carried into effect suggestions which had been made by various organizations in the Peace river country.
I think I should make it crystal clear that this is not a case of an argument between two towns as to which should have a post office constructed or as to which one should get an airfield. There is a very great and considerable measure of principle involved. Are we going to open up the development of northern Canada for the benefit of a few large privileged companies, or is this development to be for the advantage of the people of Canada? This is not the time or place to argue the pros and cons of the respective alternative routes, but there is no doubt that the Canadian Pacific and Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and two large lumber companies have come out very strongly in favour of one route, as has also the Social Credit government in Alberta, if we are to judge from the report of the provincially appointed MacGregor commission. However, the Alberta government did become alarmed at the public outcry and ultimately reversed its stand in a somewhat weak and tepid fashion. But up until slightly more than a year ago it did appear as if these people were going to have their way and cause the breach of a solemn covenant and undertaking made over 25 years ago and which led, in a large measure, to the settlement of the northern part of the lands drained by the Peace river.
Now, all this has been said before, and I am not going to labour the point. I want to make it clear that northern development must not be thought of as a one-way street down which is to flow the spoils of the north country. If we take out the capital goods of our natural resources we must replace them with something of equal value which can and should include people, settlement and industrialization, all of a permanent nature. It seems to me this would be a good place to refer to an issue which relates to my remarks and which I think is also pertinent to the item under discussion. When I was making inquiries over a year ago on this particular issue I was, to some extent, puzzled because the proponents of the eastern route seemed to feel that from the viewpoint of revenue there would be a great deal more to be expected from the McMurray route from lumber and lumber products than from the western route. My belief had been different, but I had not taken into calculation the timber from the great Wood Buffalo national park, which is one of the largest parks in

the world and lies partly in the province of Alberta and partly in the Northwest Territories.
I subsequently discovered that it was in this park that the timber resources were alleged to be. At a meeting of the mines, forests and waters committee during the last session, I asked one of the officials of the department a question-I think this was reported in the proceedings of July 7, 1958- and I received the information that there were approximately 1,200 million board feet of commercial timber and pulp along the Peace river estuary in this park. This session I put question No. 245 on the order paper to find out just what formed the legal basis for the commercial exploitation of lumber resources in this park because I always had been of the impression that the lumber and timber resources in a national park were not susceptible to commercial development on such a large scale. The answer to my question was given on April 28, and a synopsis of the answer indicates that the legal authority for the granting of the timber rights in the park lay in five orders in council made between August 1, 1955 and March 12, 1957.
My view, and I am not going to argue this here ad nauseam, is that each of these orders in council is, under the interpretation in the National Parks Act, quite invalid, and that licences should not have been granted in that way. If they were granted at all, it should have been done by means of a proper amendment to the act. The answers also show that the licences were granted to two companies named the Denney Logging Company Limited and the Swanson Lumber Company Limited. They secured timber berths for 1J billion board feet which constitutes most of the merchantable timber in the park.
Now, very briefly, Mr. Chairman, the National Parks Act, of which I believe the pertinent section is section 4, charter 189 of the Revised Statutes of 1952, says this:
The parks are hereby dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment, subject to the provisions of this act and the regulations, and such parks shall be maintained and made use of so as to leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.
Section 6 provides that the governor in council may authorize the sale, lease or other disposition of public lands within a park, for certain reasons, such as the requirement for the right of way or station grounds of any railway or the right of way of an oil or gas pipe line or any similar facilities.
The only means by which these orders in council could have been made for the purpose of granting these timber rights would be under section 7 which makes provision
Supply-Northern Affairs for the governor in council to make regulations for, and then in subsection (i), paragraph (iii) it states:
(Iii) the cutting and removal of dead or diseased timber and such green timber as may be necessary for the protection and management of forests in a park,-
My submission here is that these are limiting words "forest protection management" and there cannot be encompassed into this small space the rights which were here given to exploit commercially timber resources amounting to one and a half billion board feet purely under the limiting subsection of forest protection and management.
I am not taking exception to the proper development of that area. If and when it is necessary and is essential I think it should be done. I think it should be done but should have been done properly. I think that was a time when there should have probably have been an amendment to the act. I have here one of the orders in council. I am not going to go into all of them. They are all of a kind. This one is dated May 24, 1956 and refers to the fact that the committee of the privy council have had before them a report from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources:
That application has been made by Mr. R. B. Denney, Jr., of Healdsburg, California, U.S.A., for permission to cut timber on two parcels on both sides of the Peace river, including certain timbered islands lying between 112 degrees 00 minutes and 114 degrees 00 minutes west longitude;-
By the way I may say that I looked that up on the map and it covers an area of approximately 102 miles on both sides of the Peace river. The paragraph continues:
-one parcel contains approximately 192 square miles and the other approximately 24 square miles, containing approximately 700 million feet board measure of mature white spruce and approximately 150 million feet board measure of mature poplar;-
Those are miniature principalities. I think there should have been an amendment to the act in order to have amputated areas to that extent from one of our national parks. I think there is further complexity to this issue because by what is known as the Alberta Natural Resources Act of 1930 the natural resources which had until then been held by Canada or by the crown in the right of Canada were transferred to the provincial government of Alberta but there was retained all the natural resources within the limits of any national park which included Wood Buffalo national park. There was appended to that statute an agreement which was ultimately signed by both Canada and Alberta and became enacted by statutes in both jurisdictions. Section 14 of that agreement says, -I will just give a digest of it-that the parks mentioned in the schedule will remain

Supply-Northern Affairs the property of Canada and include the natural resources, which of course includes the timber. Then it goes on to say this:
-but in the event of the parliament of Canada at any time declaring that the said lands or any part thereof are no longer required for park purposes, the land, mines, minerals . . . specified in any such declaration, shall forthwith upon the making thereof belong to the province-[DOT]
Very simply and briefly I may say that I think it is quite anomalous and was quite anomalous at the time, for a federal government to be concerned in the administration of the natural resources of a large area within the limits of any provincial jurisdiction. This is a problem which of course the minister inherited and it is a difficult one having in mind that there are vested interests. I think it is possibly a question where some examination might be made of this particular section and negotiations arranged with the provincial government so that if there is to be commercial development not only of timber resources but of mineral resources in that park, then it might well be in the hands of the provincial government. I do not subscribe to the beliefs of the provincial government of Alberta but I think that is a point which I am compelled to take up.
Finally, it is because of facts like these that I think it is most essential that there should be a fair, impartial, unbiased examination of the issues involved in connection with the construction of this railroad. Others have looked at the problem but I feel that none of them have been entirely free from prejudice. Fortunately at this time the composition of the present government and the known respect of the Prime Minister for the rights of the ordinary man have been factors which have led to the appointment of the Manning inquiry. I am confident that from this inquiry will come a proper appreciation of the problems which are involved in the construction of this particular development program.
May I here make some mention of the fact that the hon. member for Mackenzie River did suggest that the railroad should be commenced and should run from Grimshaw. It is, of course, a fact that is appreciated by the people in my particular constituency. But I would make this point clear. We have never asked for anything to which we are not entitled. We think that the construction of this railroad was promised many years ago. We think that it is necessary and essential for the proper development of the Canadian north. I am quite confident that the reports and briefs which will be submitted to this commission will justify my expectations.
Finally, I think that our whole scheme of northern development is in issue here and I think as a suggested theme I can do no better


than quote what appeared on the frontispiece of the MacGregor report to which I have already referred. I do not need to apologize for plagiarism here; there is no copyright on this quotation. I will just put it on record:
And Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan, and said unto them,-
See the land, what it is; and the people that dwelleth therein, whether they be strong or weak, few or many;
And what the land is that they dwell in, whether it be good or bad; and what cities they be that they dwell in, whether in tents, or in strongholds; And what the land is, whether it be fat or lean, whether there be wood therein, or not.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like any other member, when I wanted to enquire whether the federal government was participating in the building of a bridge in a city I thought the question was to be asked of the Minister of Public Works. Hence on March 4 I asked if he could tell me whether the bridge at Prince Albert is to be paid for entirely by the federal government or whether the provincial government is paying part of the cost. At that time, as reported at page 1595 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker said this:
If the minister is able to answer without notice he may do so, but this is a question which should more properly be put on the order paper, as it asks for statistical information.
I therefore came along later and put on the order paper a starred question. On March 11, as found at page 1829 of Hansard, I was astonished to hear the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources tell me this in answer to my question. The question was this:
1.	Has the federal government built, agreed to build or made any contribution to the cost of building a bridge across the Saskatchewan river in the city of Prince Albert?
2.	If so, what proportion of the cost of the said bridge will be paid or has been paid for by the federal government?

Then the minister of northern affairs answered and this is where I was astounded. Instead of having the answer from the Minister of Public Works I received the answer from the minister of northern affairs. He said:
1.	Yes; under the roads to resources program.
2.	Fifty per cent up to a maximum of $1,250,000.
At that time I was so surprised I could not go any further with my question. But on March 12, 1959, at page 1864 and page 1865 of Hansard, I came back to the question. I said:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. In answer to a question of mine yesterday with regard to the Prince Albert bridge over the Saskatchewan river, the minister said it was built under the roads to resources program. Does that mean what are generally called access roads?
Then the minister answered:
The roads to resources program, Mr. Speaker, has been explained in the house on several occasions. It covers the roads we are building in agreement with nine of the provinces-
That excepts Quebec.
-to open to new resource areas in these various provinces.
Then I came back:
A supplementary question. Are there any roads within or immediately outside Prince Albert in that program? What I mean is, in the program of roads are there any within the city of Prince Albert or in the immediate vicinity?
Then the minister answered:
Mr. Speaker, the main project in the agreement in the province of Saskatchewan is a road to Uranium City, of which the southern terminus is Prince Albert.
Then I came back with another question:
Does that road at the present time go any further than Lac la Ronge, which is 150 miles from the city of Prince Albert?
Then the minister answered:
I cannot give the house the exact mileage that the road has gone beyond Lac la Ronge, but I would say 30 or 40 miles at least. When the road is finished it will go 550 miles beyond.
Then the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked a question:
Might I ask the minister a further supplementary question? Is it not a fact that the only new road being built is from Lac la Ronge northward and that Lac la Ronge is some 150 miles away from the city of Prince Albert? Therefore the bridge is not anywhere near this road the minister mentioned?
The minister answered:
I can inform the hon. member that there are several roads in this program in the province of Saskatchewan.
As the minister answered that, I was wondering if I was making a great mistake in speaking of access roads or the roads to resources program. I find that in the estimates
Supply-Northern Affairs the explanation is given like this. When we speak of access roads we mean establishing forest access roads and trails for the attainment of adequate fire protection as well as other aspects of forest management. I have looked at the description given to roads to resources in accordance with the agreement, and it says:
Contributions to the provinces to assist in the development of roads leading to resources in accordance with agreements entered into by Canada and the provinces.
As you can see, Mr. Chairman, I am not opposed to the federal government participating in building a bridge in a city, or between two cities or between two provinces. This has been done before and it will be done in the future. What I am opposed to is the fact that when members of parliament think of a bridge in a city or around a city or between two provinces we never think for a moment that we will have to go and look in the estimates of the minister of northern affairs, except if the bridge is built under a roads to resources program or under access roads.
We find now that this bridge being built in the city of Prince Albert has been contributed to 50 per cent by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and we can find on the map that Lac la Ronge is at least 150 miles away from the city of Prince Albert. The road which goes straight to Lac la Ronge is one of the main roads of the province of Saskatchewan. It starts in the United States and goes straight to La Ronge on the border of Lac la Ronge, and then goes northwards to Uranium City. They are roads to resources started both by the federal government and the government of Saskatchewan. How is it possible, then, that the federal government should take the money from the department of northern affairs to build a bridge in a city? Was it a case of an apple for the teacher so that the good graces of the Prime Minister should fall upon the head and shoulders of the minister of northern affairs, or was it a case of an order given by the Prime Minister who wanted a contribution to the bridge in the city of Prince Albert? In the two cases I think the way it was presented is a case of false representation. It should have come from the Department of Public Works if it was within a city, particularly as the bridge was 150 miles away from the nearest road to resources.
If we went on in that way every member in this house could come and ask the minister of northern affairs to build bridges in their constituencies. I have a mine two miles away from Hull, so I could ask the minister to build an interprovincial bridge contributed one-quarter by the provincial government of
5C3G

Supply-Northern Affairs Ontario, one-quarter by the provincial government of Quebec, and then it will be the very same principle. The only difference would be the cost of the bridge. I do not understand why the minister should try to hide this thing from the members of the house.

date? What is the target? We will co-operate right down the line but we want some understanding.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
As the hon. member knows, the government is not in a position to say when the house will be prorogued. This is almost entirely in the hands of the opposition, as I know myself from long experience on the other side. The rules of the house say that the sittings should end at ten o'clock. Mind you, it would always be possible for the government to bring in a motion changing the hours of sitting but we have no intention of doing that.
As I pointed out last week, we had hoped that the session would end by a week from tomorrow. It is with this thought in mind that I took the liberty this evening of asking the committee to carry on until, let us say, eleven o'clock, with these estimates. There is no agreement to be enforced. This is entirely in the judgment of hon. members themselves. That has been the case each evening when the house has sat beyond the normal closing hour of ten o'clock. If hon. members of the C.C.F. do not want to stay beyond ten o'clock, certainly there is no intention of forcing them to do so. If we wished to force them it would be quite impossible to do so.
